sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Relations between Japan and the United States worsened through the 1930s over China. Japan took Manchuria in 1931 and began a war to conquer China in 1937; in 1940 it joined the Axis and by 1941 it had occupied all of Indochina. The United States aided China, strengthened its forces in the Pacific and, in July 1941, froze Japanese assets and embargoed oil and other war materials.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Japan, poor in natural resources, saw the embargo on oil as a threat to its survival and resolved to seize the resource-rich territories of Southeast Asia, although this would mean war with the United States. The Japanese records trace the decision step by step: on 6 September 1941 an Imperial Conference resolved, in the name of “self-existence and self-preservation”, to complete preparations for war with the United States, Britain and the Netherlands by the end of October while negotiating, and to go to war if its demands were not met by early October. Negotiations continued through the autumn, but after the Hull Note of 27 November Prime Minister Tōjō Hideki's government gave up hope of a settlement, and on 1 December an Imperial Conference decided on war; Tōjō argued that war was the only way out.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Admiral Yamamoto Isoroku, commander of the Combined Fleet, planned a surprise attack to immobilise the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor at the outset of the war, so that the Japanese conquest of Southeast Asia and the East Indies could proceed unhindered. Its key elements were meticulous preparation, surprise, and carriers and naval aviation used on an unprecedented scale.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Pearl Harbor on Oahu was the base of the Pacific Fleet, with its battleships moored along Battleship Row by Ford Island and Army and Navy airfields around the island. The Japanese task force crossed the North Pacific away from normal shipping lanes to a point north of Oahu.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Vice Admiral Nagumo Chūichi commanded the striking force of six heavy aircraft carriers with supporting ships, and submarines were deployed to attack any ships that escaped. At Pearl Harbor command was shared by Admiral Husband E. Kimmel and Lieutenant General Walter C. Short. The US aircraft carriers were away: Enterprise and Lexington were ferrying aircraft to Wake and Midway, and Saratoga was on the West Coast.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Kimmel and Short had been warned of the possibility of war, with a war warning on 27 November. Short ordered an alert against sabotage and parked his aircraft close together; Kimmel did not extend reconnaissance to the north-west and kept most of the fleet in harbour. Neither expected the base itself to be attacked. Nagumo's fleet left the Kurile Islands in secrecy on 26 November, five days before the Imperial Conference formally decided on war.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At 6 a.m. on 7 December the carriers launched the first wave. Early warnings, a submarine attacked by the destroyer Ward and a radar sighting at Opana, were not acted on. Shortly before 8 a.m. the aircraft struck the airfields, destroying many aircraft on the ground, and the battleships: Arizona exploded, Oklahoma capsized and West Virginia and California sank. A second wave at about 8.50 attacked Nevada as she tried to leave the harbour; she was beached to keep the channel clear. The attack ended before 10 a.m., and the Japanese task force withdrew without being attacked.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Yamamoto's plan staked everything on surprise and carrier aviation. Kimmel's decision to send carriers to Wake and Midway saved them; Short's anti-sabotage precautions left aircraft packed together and easy to destroy. The Japanese left the shore facilities of the naval base and the oil storage undamaged; the Naval History and Heritage Command notes that the shore facilities played an important role in the Allied victory.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Complete surprise in the first minutes decided the attack: most of the damage to the battleships was done in the first half hour. What was not hit proved equally important: the carriers were absent, and the shore installations survived.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Twenty-one ships of the Pacific Fleet were sunk or damaged and a great many aircraft were destroyed, most before they could take off; Japanese losses were light. Americans killed included civilians. All but three of the damaged ships, Arizona, Oklahoma and Utah, were eventually raised or repaired.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The attack united a divided nation and swept away support for neutrality; on 8 December Congress declared war on Japan. Kimmel and Short were relieved, and the disaster led to numerous investigations.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A brilliant tactical surprise can be a strategic error: the attack brought into the war an enemy whose industrial and political strength Japan could not match. What a strike leaves untouched, carriers, fuel and repair yards, can matter more than what it destroys. Warnings are only useful if they are interpreted correctly.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica records a wide divergence of opinion on responsibility: the Roberts Commission blamed Kimmel and Short, the army and navy boards blamed the War and Navy Departments, and the 1946 congressional majority stressed the lack of preparation in Hawaii. It reports that the “back door to war” theory, that Roosevelt invited the attack, found little support among mainstream historians and was further undermined by declassified code-breaking documents, and that there is substantial evidence that he sought to postpone a clash. The Japanese conference records published by JACAR show the decision for war taking shape over three months, with a deadline set in September and the final decision taken after the Hull Note. The brief's question of a third strike is not discussed in the sources read; the Naval History and Heritage Command notes only that the shore facilities were not attacked.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Naval History and Heritage Command's overview gives the background, the plan, the approach, the attack, the losses and the salvage. Britannica gives the diplomatic background, the warnings and responses, the attack and the investigations. Two of JACAR's commentaries on Japanese government documents give the Imperial Conferences of 6 September and 1 December 1941.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the First World War Britain built a naval base at Singapore and emplaced coastal guns against attack from the sea, but no permanent fleet was based there; a fleet was to be sent only when a threat was imminent. Newspapers and politicians called the island an impregnable fortress, the Gibraltar of the East, although its defences had been underfunded for years.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Bogged down in China and cut off from American, British and Dutch oil, Japan resolved to seize the resources of the Dutch East Indies, and it needed Singapore as a base for that advance. The attack on Malaya was part of a wider offensive launched at the same time as Pearl Harbor. Most senior British planners accepted that the island could not be held if the Malayan mainland was lost.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Japanese aimed to advance down the Malay Peninsula and take Singapore from the landward side. The Twenty-Fifth Army's units, drawn from Japan, Manchuria and China, were first assembled on Hainan, carried some 2,000 kilometres by sea to land at the northern end of the peninsula, and were then to fight their way some 1,100 kilometres to Singapore; the plan allowed a hundred days. The British planned a pre-emptive move into Thailand, Operation Matador, which political considerations prevented from being launched in time, and otherwise relied on the jungle and on defence of the peninsula.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Malay Peninsula is long and covered by jungle, and the main Japanese advance came down its western side. Singapore island is separated from the mainland by the Johor Strait, crossed by the Causeway; the island's coastal guns faced the sea, and the Bukit Timah heights held its supply depots and, with the reservoirs, its water.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Lieutenant General Tomoyuki Yamashita commanded the Japanese Twenty-Fifth Army, well trained and with many more tanks and aircraft. Lieutenant General Arthur Percival commanded British, Australian, Indian and Malay troops who outnumbered the attackers but had little experience, especially of jungle warfare; the IWM notes that British planning was also shaped by racist stereotypes of the Japanese. Force Z, the battleship Prince of Wales and the battlecruiser Repulse, had been sent as a deterrent without the aircraft carrier meant to accompany it.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Percival spread his troops across the whole peninsula, so that the Japanese outnumbered them at the landing places. On Singapore island he expected the attack east of the Causeway, where the naval base lay, and placed his strongest forces there.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 8 December 1941 Japanese troops landed at Singora and Patani in Thailand and at Kota Bharu in Malaya, and bombs fell on Singapore. Japanese aircraft attacked the RAF airfields, and on 10 December sank Prince of Wales and Repulse, which had no air cover; Captain Sonokawa, who led one of the naval air groups based near Saigon, later said that a submarine had reported the ships the day before, that his aircraft had been loading bombs for an attack on Singapore and were re-armed with torpedoes, and that a night attack was tried because it was feared the ships would attack the invasion transports. Using bicycles, motor vehicles and light tanks, the Japanese outmanoeuvred the defenders down the length of the peninsula, and the last British troops crossed the Causeway on 31 January 1942. On the night of 8 February, after a heavy bombardment, Japanese divisions crossed the Johor Strait in the north-west against the Australian sector, and the Imperial Guards followed at Kranji. They took Bukit Timah on 11 February. On 14–15 February Japanese troops massacred patients and staff at the Alexandra Military Hospital. With the reservoirs lost and water and food running out, Percival and his commanders decided to surrender, and he signed at the Ford Factory on 15 February.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Percival's dispersal of his forces down the peninsula and his misreading of where the Japanese would land on the island let the attackers concentrate where it mattered. Yamashita chose to attack with three divisions rather than four and drove his troops on at speed; by the end, the IWM notes, he had outrun his supplies and was short of ammunition, and he insisted on unconditional surrender for fear that the British would discover his weakness. Churchill ordered Singapore held to the last man, a political rather than a military imperative.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of Prince of Wales and Repulse on 10 December and of air cover over Malaya decided the campaign's course; on the island, the landing in the north-west on 8 February and the loss of Bukit Timah, with its depots and water, left Percival unable to hold out.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Singapore fell on 15 February 1942 in the largest surrender in British history. Malaya had been lost in under two months; the Japanese National Institute for Defense Studies notes that Singapore was taken in 70 days, earlier than the hundred the plan had allowed.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: From 21 February to 4 March 1942, in Operation Sook Ching, Chinese men aged 18 to 50 were ordered to screening centres across the island on the directive of Yamashita, and those whom the Kempeitai or the Imperial Guards judged anti-Japanese, often arbitrarily, were taken to beaches and remote places such as Changi, Punggol and Bedok and machine-gunned; thousands were killed, and the true number is unknown. The prisoners taken at Singapore were treated brutally; many were held at Changi, and others were sent to build the Burma–Thailand railway. Civilians suffered food shortages and conscription under the occupation. The loss began the long decline of British prestige in Asia, and Australia turned increasingly to the United States.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Speed and initiative can defeat a larger but inexperienced and dispersed defender. Capital ships without air cover are vulnerable to aircraft. A fortress that exists mainly in propaganda, without the fleet, aircraft and landward defences it depends on, cannot be held once its approaches are lost.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The IWM argues that Percival made mistakes but was badly let down by superiors who had underfunded the defences for years. The sources qualify the popular idea that Singapore's guns pointed the wrong way: the IWM notes that the coastal artillery was designed against attack from the sea and had few high-explosive shells, while the National Library Board notes that the British army had anticipated a landward attack and planned Operation Matador to meet it. The sources give different strengths for the two armies, and Sonokawa's figures for the attack on Force Z are not used. The National Library Board notes that the death toll of the Sook Ching is unknown, with estimates differing widely.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Imperial War Museums' account by Stephen Walton gives the strategic background, the forces, the campaign, the surrender and its consequences. The National Library Board of Singapore's Infopedia gives the battle for the island, the Alexandra Hospital massacre and the surrender, and, in a separate article, Operation Sook Ching and its aftermath. The Japanese side comes from the National Institute for Defense Studies of Japan's Ministry of Defense, in Japanese, which outlines the Twenty-Fifth Army's plan from its own record of the operation, and from the U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey's interrogation of Captain Sonokawa on the sinking of Force Z.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Pearl Harbor Japanese forces expanded rapidly across the Pacific and South-east Asia. By April 1942 Japan had established a defensive perimeter and sought to extend it.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Japan planned to advance south-east from the Bismarcks and Solomons and seize control of the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, establishing air bases at Port Moresby in New Guinea and Tulagi in the Solomons. Allied signals intelligence uncovered the plan to take Port Moresby, and all available Allied sea and air power was alerted.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Japanese aimed to take Tulagi and then land at Port Moresby, with a carrier strike force to find and destroy the Allied naval forces that came to oppose them. Captain Yamaoka, a staff officer aboard Zuikaku, later gave the fleet carriers three tasks: to cover the Port Moresby invasion group, to attack the American fleet expected to appear, and to raid Townsville in Australia; the light carrier Shōhō was to guard the transports against submarines and air attack. The Allies aimed to stop the invasion of Port Moresby.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought over the Coral Sea, between New Guinea, the Solomons and Australia. The opposing carrier forces searched for each other over wide areas of ocean, and their ships never came within sight of each other.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Two US carrier task forces, built around Yorktown and Lexington under Rear Admiral Frank J. Fletcher, and a combined US–Australian cruiser force that included HMAS Australia and Hobart, faced the Japanese Carrier Strike Force with the fleet carriers Shōkaku and Zuikaku, supporting units and the invasion force from Rabaul, and the light carrier Shōhō.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: When the Japanese landed at Tulagi on 3 May, aircraft from Fletcher's task force struck the landing group on 4 May. The invasion force left Rabaul for Port Moresby, and its covering units took a route that invited a clash with Fletcher. The Allied cruisers were detached to guard against the Port Moresby invasion force.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 5 and 6 May the carrier groups searched for each other; Yamaoka says the Japanese knew from the attack on Tulagi that an American force was in the area but not where. On the morning of 7 May Japanese scout planes reported the oiler Neosho and the destroyer Sims as the American carriers, and Japanese carrier aircraft sank them, while Fletcher's aircraft sank the light carrier Shōhō and a cruiser. A Japanese dusk strike found nothing and, returning in the dark, passed over the American carriers; some of its planes tried to land on them before realising their mistake. On 8 May both sides struck at each other's carriers: Japanese aircraft sank Lexington, which was abandoned after explosions and fires, and damaged Yorktown, while US aircraft damaged Shōkaku so badly that she had to retire. With its air cover weakened and under attack by Allied land-based bombers, the Port Moresby invasion force turned back to Rabaul.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Acting on intelligence, the Allies committed their carriers to meet the Japanese advance. Both sides made many mistakes in the new kind of fighting; the Naval History and Heritage Command quotes Samuel Eliot Morison calling it a battle of errors in which the enemy made more and failed to profit by them. On the night of 7 May the Japanese, without radar and unsure how many American ships there were, declined a night action and retired north to attack in the morning; Yamaoka says he had wanted to attack that night. Sekino and Okumiya say the invasion force turned back because the American task force had not been destroyed and the remaining Japanese force, with the main fleet just back from the Indian Ocean, was not strong enough to attempt the landing. That decision, once the air groups were too battered to cover the landing, decided the outcome.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The heavy losses of Japanese aircraft and the damage to Shōkaku left the Japanese unable to cover the landing at Port Moresby, and the invasion was called off.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Japanese sank more ships, and the Naval History and Heritage Command calls the battle a Japanese tactical victory. But Port Moresby remained in Allied hands, and Britannica calls the battle a strategic Allied victory. It was the first time since Pearl Harbor that the Japanese advance had been checked.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Shōkaku was too badly damaged to join the force for Midway, and Zuikaku, having lost pilots and aircraft, did not take part either; Coral Sea reduced the carriers available to Japan for Midway by a third. The Japanese officers interrogated in 1945 confirmed that the damage weakened the air striking force at Midway and that the sea-borne attack on Port Moresby was given up, so that the army tried to take it overland from the north coast of New Guinea. It was the first naval battle in which the ships never sighted or fired at each other, and it foreshadowed the carrier warfare of the rest of the Pacific War.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A tactical draw, or even a tactical defeat, can be a strategic victory if it stops the enemy's purpose. Intelligence that reveals the enemy's objective allows a weaker force to be in the right place. In carrier warfare, reconnaissance under uncertainty decides who strikes first and at what.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources judge the outcome differently: the Naval History and Heritage Command calls it a Japanese tactical victory that nonetheless stopped the advance, Britannica a strategic Allied victory. The Naval History and Heritage Command dates the operations from 29 April, Britannica and the Australian War Memorial the battle from 4 May. The Japanese officers' answers were given to American interrogators in October 1945 and are recollections: they differ in details, Yamaoka misdates the 7 May attack to June, and their figures for losses are not used. Sekino was not sure why no night attack was made, while Yamaoka says it was rejected for lack of information about American strength.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Naval History and Heritage Command gives the Japanese plan, the air strikes, the losses and the battle's effect on Midway. Britannica gives the intelligence, the course of the battle and its strategic result. The Australian War Memorial gives the Allied forces, including the Australian cruisers, and the turning back of the invasion force. The interrogations of Commanders Sekino and Okumiya and of Captain Yamaoka by the U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey in October 1945, transcribed by HyperWar, give the Japanese side.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Pearl Harbor Japan occupied islands across the western Pacific as a defensive buffer. The victories at the Coral Sea and Midway in the spring of 1942 meant that the Japanese navy could no longer mount major offensives, and the Allies could begin their own. In July 1942 Japanese troops and labourers began building an airfield on Guadalcanal in the southern Solomons.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Aircraft based on the new airfield would threaten Allied bases in the New Hebrides and New Caledonia, Port Moresby and the supply routes to Australia and New Zealand. The Allies took immediate steps to eject the Japanese with the forces available in the South Pacific.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Allies aimed to seize the airfield on Guadalcanal and the harbour at Tulagi and hold them. The Japanese aimed to retake the airfield, reinforcing the island by sea and bombarding the field, and to defeat the American naval forces that supported it.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Guadalcanal is a jungle-covered island in the southern Solomons. The airfield, renamed Henderson Field, lay at Lunga Point; across the sound lay Florida Island and Tulagi. Rabaul, the main Japanese base in the region, lay some 1,050 kilometres to the north-west, while aircraft at Henderson Field could strike ships in the surrounding waters. The jungle, the weather and the lack of infrastructure made supply and movement extremely difficult.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The 1st Marine Division under Major General Alexander Vandegrift made the landing, supported by naval task forces; it was later reinforced and in December relieved by US Army divisions. Vice Admiral Robert Ghormley commanded the naval forces in the South Pacific until Vice Admiral William Halsey succeeded him on 18 October. The aircraft at Henderson Field, the “Cactus Air Force”, combined Marine, Navy and Army aviators. On the Japanese side, the Seventeenth Army fought on the island, supported by the fleet; Rear Admiral Tanaka Raizō's destroyers ran the night reinforcement convoys known as the Tokyo Express.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 7–8 August 1942 the Marines landed on Guadalcanal, Tulagi and neighbouring islands in the US Navy's first offensive amphibious operation in the Pacific. They met little resistance on Guadalcanal and took the almost complete airfield within about a day and a half, while the Japanese defenders of Tulagi fought almost to the last man. Vandegrift formed a tight perimeter around Henderson Field.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On the night of 8–9 August Japanese cruisers surprised the Allied screening force off Savo Island, sank three American cruisers and crippled an Australian one, the worst defeat in a single fleet action suffered by the US Navy. The Japanese then counterattacked on land, at the Tenaru in August and at Edson's Ridge on 13–14 September, and at sea, in the carrier battle of the Eastern Solomons on 24 August, after which a Japanese reinforcement convoy that had lost its air support was ordered back. Cape Esperance on 11–12 October and the carrier battle of Santa Cruz on 26 October, a Japanese tactical victory that cost them heavily in aircrew, accompanied a major Japanese ground offensive against the Henderson perimeter on 23–26 October, which failed. In the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal on 12–15 November the US Navy blocked Japan's last major attempt to retake the island from the sea. At Tassafaronga on 30 November Tanaka's destroyers, surprised by American cruisers while preparing to land supplies, turned away and fired a mass torpedo attack, damaging American cruisers and losing one destroyer. From then on American reinforcements outpaced Japanese ones, and at the end of December the Japanese high command accepted the case for evacuation, which began in late January; the last troops were taken off by destroyers on the night of 7 February 1943.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Vandegrift's decision to concentrate his Marines in a tight perimeter around the airfield kept the key to the campaign in American hands, and warning from code-breakers helped him meet the first attacks. Japanese commanders, believing after Savo Island that most Americans had withdrawn, underestimated the garrison. At Savo Island itself, Rear Admiral Matsuyama, a passenger aboard the cruiser Tenryū, later said the mission had been to attack the transports, but the orders were simply to pass around Savo Island, fire on the ships and go home. Captain Toyama, Tanaka's chief of staff, says the August convoy was ordered back because the loss of Ryūjō left it without air support, and that at Tassafaronga he ordered his destroyers not to open fire with guns unless necessary and to make a mass torpedo attack. Halsey concentrated his carriers for Santa Cruz, and in November the US Navy accepted heavy losses in night actions to stop the reinforcement convoys.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The repulse of the October ground offensive and the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal in November decided the campaign: after November the Japanese could no longer seriously threaten Henderson Field, and the Tokyo Express could no longer operate with impunity. A Japanese officer reportedly called the November battle the fork in the road.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Guadalcanal was in Allied hands by February 1943, and the American positions in the southern Solomons were never again seriously threatened. Both sides lost many ships in the waters off the island, which became known as Ironbottom Sound; the Japanese also lost aircraft and experienced aircrew they could not replace.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Together with Midway, the Naval History and Heritage Command judges, the victory on Guadalcanal was probably the turning point of the Pacific War, and Japan was now on the defensive. It was the first step in the Allied advance that went on through the Gilbert, Marshall and Mariana Islands to Iwo Jima and Okinawa. American troops suffered heavily from malaria and other tropical diseases, and the Japanese troops on the island were weakened as their supply failed.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An island base is only as strong as its air cover and the ability to supply it; whoever could reinforce faster would hold Guadalcanal. In a campaign of attrition the stronger industrial power gains by accepting battle repeatedly, as long as it holds the key position. Intelligence, surface night-fighting skill and the use of a single airfield shaped the outcome as much as any one battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the end differently: the Naval History and Heritage Command gives the last evacuation on the night of 7 February, Britannica the elimination of the last pocket on 8 February. They also give different totals for losses on both sides. The National WWII Museum stresses early American mistakes in moving supplies inland, while Britannica stresses the success of the initial landing. The Japanese officers' accounts were recorded by American interrogators in late 1945. Matsuyama had no access to the battle plans, and the interrogators noted that part of his account came from conversation after the battle; why the cruisers left without attacking the transports is not explained by it.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the naval and land campaigns in detail, from the landings to the evacuation. The National WWII Museum gives the strategic setting, the October offensive and the campaign's significance. sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Britain depended on supplies from North America and the Empire carried across the Atlantic in merchant ships, which German submarines (U-boats) and surface warships could attack. The German navy had begun building a modern U-boat arm in 1936, and the German Historical Museum's LeMO notes that its task under Karl Dönitz was to sink the convoys carrying supplies and war material to Britain, but a total blockade was never achieved. The first Atlantic convoy sailed on 2 September 1939. After the fall of France in June 1940 the U-boats gained bases on the French Atlantic coast, and from August 1940, when unrestricted submarine warfare was declared in the waters around the British Isles as part of the plans to invade England, British shipping losses became heavy. Churchill coined the name the Battle of the Atlantic in March 1941.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: For the Allies the battle meant blockading the Axis, securing their own sea movements and being able to project military power across the ocean; Churchill saw it as Germany's best chance to defeat the Western powers. Any invasion of Europe depended on carrying troops and supplies across the Atlantic. When the United States entered the war, U-boats sank many unescorted ships off its east coast in early 1942 until convoys were introduced.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Grand Admiral Karl Dönitz, commander of the U-boat arm and later of the whole German navy, aimed to frustrate the Allied use of the Atlantic by sinking merchant shipping. The Allies aimed to deliver their convoys safely and, increasingly, to destroy the U-boats attacking them.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Atlantic covers more than 100 million square kilometres, so that a convoy was hard to find. In the mid-Atlantic, beyond the reach of most land-based aircraft, lay the air gap where convoys had no air cover and were most vulnerable. U-boats returning to the French bases had to cross the Bay of Biscay.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Allies grouped merchant ships into convoys escorted by warships and, where possible, aircraft; British, Canadian and, from 1941, American navies and air forces shared the escort of the North Atlantic. Dönitz, head of the U-boat arm since 1936, directed his U-boats by radio from his headquarters, assembling them into groups, the wolf packs, on patrol lines across the convoy routes. The Bundesarchiv's guide shows how his operations staff directed the boats in the North Sea, the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean from successive headquarters, at Kernevel near Lorient from 1940 to 1942, then Paris, Berlin and, from 1943, Bernau near Berlin. LeMO adds that the navy had no reconnaissance aircraft of its own, so the boats had to find their targets by forming a patrol line, and that once a group attacked, each commander had full freedom of action. Both sides fought a war of intelligence: German code-breakers read British convoy codes from 1941 into 1943, while the British read naval Enigma traffic until a fourth rotor was added in February 1942.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: By May 1941 a fully escorted transatlantic convoy system was in place, and the loss of the battleship Bismarck that month ended German surface raids. The expansion of convoys in the western hemisphere forced the U-boats back into the mid-Atlantic by late 1942, where the battle reached its climax.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: From January to July 1942, LeMO writes, the U-boats operating off the American east coast, where coastal defences were weak, had the most successful period of the war, sinking ships even off New York and the mouth of the Mississippi. The crisis peaked in March 1943, when the Allies again lost the ability to read U-boat signals for a time and U-boats sank great numbers of ships in a few weeks. By then decisions of the Casablanca Conference had begun to push naval and air reinforcements into the North Atlantic. In April and May improving weather, very-long-range Liberator aircraft that closed the air gap, escort carriers, roving support groups, centimetric radar, high-frequency direction-finding and new weapons such as the Hedgehog and an air-dropped homing torpedo came together. In early May the escorts of convoy ONS-5 beat off repeated attacks. U-boat losses became unsustainable, and on 24 May Dönitz withdrew his U-boats from the North Atlantic, while ordering the war to continue in the South Atlantic and the Indian Ocean. Renewed attacks with acoustic torpedoes in the autumn failed, and for the rest of the war the Allies controlled the Atlantic sea-lanes.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Allied decision to give anti-submarine production top priority, and the decisions at Casablanca to reinforce the North Atlantic, provided the ships, aircraft and escort carriers that turned the battle. Dönitz's central control of the wolf packs by radio, which the Germans believed secure, exposed them to direction-finding even when their codes could not be read. His recall order of 24 May accepted that his losses were no longer matched by sinkings.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: May 1943, known as Black May, was the turning point: U-boat losses rose sharply while sinkings fell. The Naval History and Heritage Command notes that by then American shipyards were producing far more ships than the Germans could sink, while the Germans were losing more submarines than they could replace.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The U-boats never regained the initiative and were almost constantly on the defensive from the autumn of 1943; LeMO calls the continued campaign increasingly hopeless and notes that most of the U-boats lost in the war were sunk after May 1943. Shipping losses fell sharply, and supplies and troops crossed to Britain for the invasion of 1944.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Atlantic was the longest campaign of the war, from September 1939 to May 1945. Victory there, with the opening of the Mediterranean to through traffic, brought significant reductions in shipping losses and allowed the build-up for the invasion of Normandy. The Naval History and Heritage Command also notes the importance of the Arctic convoys to the Soviet Union, which came at a critical time.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Success in a campaign against shipping is measured in ships delivered and ships built, not only in submarines sunk. Technology, intelligence, numbers and tactics improved by experience and scientific analysis combined to turn the battle; none alone was decisive. A side that believes its communications secure may expose itself in ways it does not suspect.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The relative weight of code-breaking against technology, air power and industry is debated. The Naval History and Heritage Command argues that no single factor was decisive and that Allied intelligence against the U-boats was at its weakest during the turning point of May 1943; Britannica lists the repenetration of the U-boat codes among the causes of the May defeat. The German Historical Museum's account explains the turn by the closing of the air gap with long-range bombers and escort carriers and by radar and sonar, and does not mention code-breaking at all. The Naval History and Heritage Command also warns that statistics for the battle should be treated with caution because sources count them differently; LeMO's figures for boats, ships and men are not used. The Bundesarchiv notes that the records of the U-boat command survive at its military archive in Freiburg and that only a few have been digitised.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Imperial War Museums give the convoy system and the course of the battle to May 1943. Samuel J. Cox's account for the Naval History and Heritage Command gives the intelligence war, the technologies, the production race and Dönitz's withdrawal. Thomas A. Hughes and Marc Milner's Britannica article gives the phases of the whole battle and its strategic importance. Arnulf Scriba's article for the German Historical Museum's LeMO and the Bundesarchiv's research guide, both in German, give the German side: the U-boat arm's aims, its tactics and the organisation and headquarters of Dönitz's command.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Pearl Harbor Japan invaded Burma, and Rangoon fell by March 1942. British and Indian forces made a fighting retreat of about 1,600 kilometres into India, the longest in British history. In November 1943 South East Asia Command was formed under Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Earlier in the war British troops had fallen back when their supply lines were cut and had largely stopped operations in the monsoon. South East Asia Command now ordered troops to stand firm, rely on air supply and keep fighting. The Japanese sought to pre-empt a planned British invasion of Burma. The Japan Center for Asian Historical Records, part of the National Archives of Japan, gives the operation's purpose as cutting the Allied supply route to Chiang Kai-shek and inciting anti-British movements in India, in collaboration with Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army. Arakawa Kenichi, of the Japanese Ministry of Defense's National Institute for Defense Studies, adds that the worsening course of the war and the Tojo government's cooperation with Bose in 1943 pushed the operation forward.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: In March 1944 the Japanese Fifteenth Army launched Operation U-Go to capture the British supply bases on the Imphal Plain and cut the Dimapur–Imphal road at Kohima. Holding Imphal would disrupt Allied air supplies to China, delay a British return to Burma and give Japan a base for attacks on India. Arakawa argues that the operation's primary objective was to protect the whole of Burma, but that Mutaguchi, prompted by the first Chindit expedition of Orde Wingate and by his own promotion to command the Fifteenth Army, added an ambitious aim of his own that put it beyond the army's capacity.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Imphal, capital of Manipur, lay on a plain ringed by hills and was the main British base in the region. Kohima, a small village on a ridge on the road from Dimapur, controlled the route by which Imphal could be relieved. The monsoon began during the battle.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Lieutenant-General Renya Mutaguchi commanded three Japanese divisions and one Indian National Army division. Lieutenant-General William Slim's Fourteenth Army held the front: IV Corps under Geoffrey Scoones at Imphal, and XXXIII Corps under Montagu Stopford, which relieved Kohima and Imphal. Slim had rebuilt the army's morale, trained it in jungle warfare and introduced defensive boxes that could be supplied by air.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Mutaguchi expected to destroy IV Corps quickly and seize its supplies before his own logistics failed. The 33rd Division was to cut off the 17th Indian Division south of Imphal and the 15th Division to cut the road to Kohima, while the 31st Division under Kotoku Sato surrounded Kohima to block relief from Dimapur. The defenders of Kohima were a scratch garrison under Colonel Hugh Richards.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Japanese advance on Imphal began on 8 March, and on 29 March they cut the Imphal–Kohima road. By early April both Kohima and Imphal were surrounded. At Kohima the garrison, supplied by air, held a shrinking perimeter on Garrison Hill from 5 to 18 April in some of the bitterest fighting of the war, at one point separated from the Japanese only by the tennis court of the Deputy Commissioner's bungalow; the British 2nd Division broke through on 18 April. Fighting around Kohima went on until mid-May, when Sato's division began to withdraw. Japanese attacks on Imphal failed against the Indian divisions there. Despite the monsoon, the Allies counter-attacked up the road, and on 22 June XXXIII Corps linked up with IV Corps at Imphal. The battles ended on 18 July.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Slim's army stood and fought on the Imphal plain, its encircled formations supplied by air rather than retreating, as South East Asia Command now required. Mountbatten sent the 2nd Division to Dimapur, and the 5th Indian Division was flown from the Arakan to Imphal in two days. Mutaguchi gambled on capturing Allied supplies, quarrelled with his divisional commanders and kept attacking long after the offensive had clearly failed, when he could have withdrawn. Arakawa explains why the plan went ahead unchanged: conceived in the spring of 1943, it was carried out a year later without revision, because Mutaguchi's superior, Lieutenant-General Kawabe, kept a loose rein on him and Major-General Inada, the Southern Army's vice chief of staff who had urged changes, was moved; and once the operation was failing, neither Mutaguchi nor Kawabe could bring himself to halt it.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The garrison's stand at Kohima and the failure of the attacks on Imphal by early May denied the Japanese the supplies they depended on. Allied logistics and air supply, which the National Army Museum calls decisive, allowed rapid reinforcement and kept the garrisons fighting. Arakawa stresses that the British and Indian army had changed during 1943, postponing its offensive, adopting the defensive box and retraining, and that Mutaguchi did not notice or took no interest in the change.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The National Army Museum calls Imphal–Kohima one of the biggest defeats the Japanese army ever suffered. When Mutaguchi's plan to seize Allied supplies failed, his men starved during the worst of the monsoon; most of his army was killed, wounded or missing. Mutaguchi was relieved of command and forced into retirement.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory opened the way for the reconquest of Burma. The Fourteenth Army crossed the Chindwin during the monsoon, supplied by air, won bridgeheads over the Irrawaddy and took Meiktila and Mandalay in March 1945, and Rangoon fell in May. The cemeteries at Imphal and Kohima, with the Kohima Epitaph, commemorate the dead. In Japan, the weekly Shashin Shuho reported the capture of Kohima and the rapid advance with the Indian National Army; its last article on the battle, on 31 May 1944, still praised the army's achievements but described the enemy more guardedly.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Logistics decided the battle: an offensive that depends on capturing the enemy's supplies fails if the enemy holds, while air supply allowed encircled troops to stand. Morale, training and confidence restored by a commander can turn a defeated army into a winning one. Persisting with a failed offensive turns a setback into a disaster.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources give different loss figures; JACAR's are not used. Both the National Army Museum and the Imperial War Museums call the battle a turning point, but the Imperial War Museums note that it is among the lesser-known battles of the war. The British sources mention the Indian National Army only as one division under Mutaguchi; the Japanese archive's account makes cooperation with it, and the hope of stirring anti-British movements in India, part of the operation's purpose. Arakawa's paper, given at the Japanese Ministry of Defense's forum on war history in 2002 and read here in its English summary, traces the disaster to Mutaguchi's excessive sense of mission and to a command system that let his plan go unrevised, a judgement close to the British sources' view of Mutaguchi.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the background, the commanders, the plans, the sieges, the air supply and the aftermath, and in a separate article Slim's methods. The Imperial War Museums give Operation U-Go, the siege of Kohima, the link-up and the outcome. The Japan Center for Asian Historical Records gives the Japanese purpose and the wartime reporting of the battle, and the English summary of Arakawa Kenichi's paper for the National Institute for Defense Studies gives a Japanese analysis of Mutaguchi's plan and the command decisions behind it.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the spring of 1944 the tide on the Eastern Front had turned, and German strength was in irreversible decline. Soviet officers had developed a doctrine of deep battle: successive breakthroughs at several points, through which mobile forces would drive into the enemy's rear and destroy his ability to fight. The Red Army aimed to inflict on the Germans a catastrophe on the scale of Barbarossa.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Western Allies were about to land in France, and Bagration was launched in support of the Normandy invasion. Hitler wanted to hold as much territory in the east as possible until the landings in the west had been defeated, and Army Group Centre, holding a great salient in Belorussia, was forbidden to retreat. The German Historical Museum's LeMO notes that Hitler repeatedly rejected the urgent proposals of the Wehrmacht's leaders to withdraw from the salient, about 1,000 kilometres long, around Vitebsk, Orsha, Mogilev and Bobruisk.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Soviet plan, named by Stalin after Prince Pyotr Bagration, who fell at Borodino in 1812, was a succession of attacks by four fronts to encircle and destroy the German forces in the Belorussian salient and open the way to the pre-war Soviet border. Stalin gave his commanders more autonomy than in earlier offensives. A Belarusian state archive's account gives the Soviet view of the plan: drawn up by the General Staff of the Red Army and approved by the Supreme Command at the end of May, it set the 1st Baltic and three Belorussian fronts the tasks of eliminating the salient on the Vitebsk–Bobruisk–Minsk axis, destroying Army Group Centre and liberating the whole of Soviet Belorussia, with cooperation between the fronts and the partisan brigades of great importance.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Belorussian salient lay north of the Pripet Marshes, the best-fortified sector of the German front, with Vitebsk, Orsha, Mogilev and Bobruisk forward and Minsk behind. German communications were long and exposed to partisans; Soviet communications were shorter. The marshes were believed impassable to heavy vehicles.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Field Marshal Ernst Busch's Army Group Centre consisted of experienced units, but German intelligence expected the Soviet summer offensive further south, against Walter Model's Army Group North Ukraine, and most German armour had been moved there. Four Soviet fronts were massed against Army Group Centre with a large advantage in men, artillery and tanks, and near-total control of the air; Konstantin Rokossovsky's armies formed the southern wing, north of the Pripet Marshes. Large partisan forces operated in the German rear.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: A deception campaign, maskirovka, disguised the Soviet build-up: civilians were moved from the front, camouflage was checked from the air and strict radio silence enforced. On the night of 19 June partisans detonated demolition charges across the railways and bridges in the German rear, hampering reinforcement. When German commanders sought to move to a more flexible defence, Busch refused.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Bagration began on 22 June, three years to the day after the German invasion. Attacks near Vitebsk on 22 June were followed on 23 June by attacks toward Orsha and Mogilev and on 24 June toward Bobruisk, behind massive barrages. Vitebsk was encircled by 24 June and Bobruisk on 27 June, where Rokossovsky's armies broke through north of the marshes. Hitler designated towns as fortified places to be held to the last man; many were bypassed and cut off. He replaced Busch with Model on 28 June, but Minsk fell on 3 July, when Soviet guards tank corps entered the city in the morning and cleared it by evening, and a large German force was trapped east of it, where fighting went on until 11 July. Vilnius fell ten days after Minsk, and the Belarusian account dates the end of the liberation of Belorussia to the capture of Brest on 28 July. The Soviets advanced into Lithuania and Poland, other offensives joined in, and on 31 July one of Rokossovsky's columns reached the suburbs of Warsaw; at the end of July Model briefly held the advance on a line from Kaunas to Brest-Litovsk. In the north the 1st Baltic Front reached the Gulf of Riga, cutting Army Group North off from East Prussia. By the first week of August the advance was halted by exhausted supply lines.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Soviet command's choice of the Belorussian salient, its deception and its readiness to shift exploitation to wherever breakthroughs succeeded, as when the 5th Guards Tank Army moved north to Vitebsk after Orsha held, turned breakthroughs into encirclements. Hitler's refusal to allow withdrawal and his fortified-place orders left German forces to be surrounded. American trucks supplied under Lend-Lease let the Soviet mobile forces move and be supplied deep in the German rear.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The encirclements at Vitebsk and Bobruisk in the first week and the fall of Minsk on 3 July, with a large German force trapped east of it, broke Army Group Centre; the IWM notes that in a few weeks it effectively ceased to exist.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Army Group Centre was destroyed, with close to 30 divisions lost, and Belorussia was liberated before the end of July. The Red Army advanced as much as 724 kilometres in five weeks, the longest and fastest advance it had yet made, reaching the Vistula and pressing deep into Lithuania. Both sides suffered very heavy losses.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: As the Red Army advanced it found mass graves of murdered civilians and razed towns and villages left by the German occupation; on 23 July, LeMO notes, it liberated the Majdanek extermination camp before the Germans could remove the crematoria, gas chambers and other evidence. German prisoners were paraded through Moscow on 17 July, and many died in Soviet labour camps. When the Polish Home Army rose in Warsaw on 1 August, the Red Army halted across the Vistula and gave no support; the Germans crushed the uprising, killed very large numbers of civilians and razed the city, a result that, Britannica notes, served Soviet purposes in Poland. LeMO likewise writes that Stalin had no interest in supporting the uprising and wanted to install the communist Lublin Committee as Poland's government. Army Group North withdrew into Courland, where it held out until the capitulation. With Overlord in the west, Bagration put the Allies in a position to crush Germany from east and west. In Belarus, 3 July, the day of Minsk's liberation, is celebrated as Independence Day.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Deep operations, multiple breakthroughs followed by rapid exploitation, could destroy an army group when combined with deception and mobility. Rigid holding orders help the attacker by leaving the defender to be encircled. An advance is limited in the end by its logistics.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the start to 22 June (Imperial War Museums, LeMO) or 23 June (Britannica, the Belarusian archive) and give different figures for German and Soviet losses; LeMO's figures for forces and losses are not used. The Imperial War Museums argue that the operation is less well known in the West than D-Day because of the Western focus on British and American operations and the Cold War. Britannica judges the halt before Warsaw intentional, and LeMO attributes it to Stalin's political aims, while the Imperial War Museums also stress Soviet exhaustion after a 700-kilometre advance. The Belarusian archive's account is a commemorative text that presents the operation as the liberation of Belarus and stresses the partisans; it is used here for the Soviet plan and the dates of liberation.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Helen Upcraft's account for the Imperial War Museums gives the doctrine, the deception, the course of the operation, the Warsaw Uprising and the debate over its place in memory. Nick Hewitt's Britannica article gives the dates, the scale and the discoveries of Nazi crimes. Basil Liddell Hart's Britannica account of the advance to the Vistula gives Rokossovsky's breakthrough and the halt before Warsaw. Arnulf Scriba's article for the German Historical Museum's LeMO, in German, gives Hitler's refusal to withdraw, the destruction of Army Group Centre and the advance to the Vistula and the Baltic. The Belarusian State Archive-Museum of Literature and Art gives the Soviet plan and the liberation of Minsk and Belorussia as remembered in Belarus.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Normandy landings and the pursuit of the German armies across France and Belgium in the summer of 1944, the Allies sought the fastest way to win the war in Europe. Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery believed that one bold stroke could shorten the war. The German front, however, was recovering: Walter Model, appointed commander in chief in the west and of Army Group B on 16 August, gave up the western command at his own request on 4 September but kept Army Group B, and, according to the Neue Deutsche Biographie, soon formed a continuous front again from the mouth of the Scheldt to Belfort.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Montgomery persuaded the Supreme Allied Commander, General Dwight D. Eisenhower, to approve a combined airborne and armoured assault through the Netherlands and to divert supplies, especially scarce fuel, to support it. In the occupied Netherlands liberation seemed weeks or even days away; the Dutch Railway Museum describes how, urged by the Allied Supreme Command, the Dutch government in London called on 17 September for a general railway strike so that the Germans could not bring troops and equipment to the battle in time.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Three airborne divisions, the US 101st and 82nd and the British 1st, were to seize the bridges along a single road through Eindhoven, Nijmegen and Arnhem (Operation Market), while XXX Corps advanced along it to cross the Rhine (Operation Garden). Success would outflank the Siegfried Line, liberate the Netherlands and open the way to the Ruhr.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The bridge at Arnhem, the farthest objective, lay about 100 kilometres from XXX Corps' start line. XXX Corps had to advance along a single narrow causeway, vulnerable to traffic jams and counter-attack, with marshes preventing movement off the road in places. Around Arnhem the wooded ground cut the range of the airborne radios.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The First Allied Airborne Army's three divisions, joined at Arnhem by the 1st Independent Polish Parachute Brigade, were lightly armed, with few heavy weapons against tanks. Major-General Roy Urquhart commanded the British 1st Airborne Division. Opposing them was Field Marshal Walter Model's Army Group B; intelligence had indicated that the area was lightly defended, but elements of two SS armoured divisions were present.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: There were too few transport aircraft to fly all the airborne troops in at once, so they were landed in three lifts, one a day. The British landing zones were about 10 kilometres west of the Arnhem bridge.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 17 September the airborne divisions landed. The 101st took most of its bridges near Eindhoven within hours, and the 82nd landed near Nijmegen. At Arnhem only the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Parachute Brigade reached the bridge and held its north end; the other battalions fought into Arnhem with heavy losses but never reached it, and the rest of the division was pressed into a pocket at Oosterbeek. XXX Corps, delayed by German defenders and blown bridges, linked up with the 82nd, and the Nijmegen bridge was taken, but the tanks did not move on for 18 hours. The battalion at the Arnhem bridge was overrun. The Polish brigade landed late and could not help, fog and low cloud hampered resupply, and German counter-attacks cut the corridor. On the night of 24–25 September the survivors of the 1st Airborne Division were ferried back across the Rhine.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Eisenhower's decision to back Montgomery's plan concentrated scarce resources on a single narrow thrust. The planners accepted landing zones far from the Arnhem bridge, a lift spread over three days and an intelligence picture of a lightly defended area. Model reacted quickly, calling for reinforcements and air support and blowing bridges along the road. In London, because the operation was secret, only Prime Minister Gerbrandy and his war minister knew of the Allied request for a railway strike; Gerbrandy agreed at once, the war minister consented despite doubts, and the call went out on Radio Orange at 17.45 on 17 September, before the rest of the cabinet and the Queen were told.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The failure to take the Arnhem bridge in strength on the first day, and XXX Corps' delays on the single road, especially at Nijmegen, decided the operation: XXX Corps could not reach Arnhem before German forces overwhelmed the British defenders.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The operation failed. All the bridges except Arnhem were captured, but most of the 1st Airborne Division was killed or captured, and the IWM records that only about a fifth of the men who dropped at Arnhem made it back.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Rhine crossing and the capture of the Ruhr were delayed by six months, and the Allies had to fight into Germany on a broad front. The operation did liberate a large part of the Netherlands south of the great rivers, but the north and west stayed under German occupation for almost eight more months. The railway strike went on all that time, yet the Germans had their own staff running military trains again after just over a week, so its military effect was small. To break the strike, Reich Commissioner Seyss-Inquart banned the transport of goods by ship; the ban was lifted in mid-October, but the rivers then froze, food stocks dwindled, especially in the west, and the result was the famine of the winter of 1944–45, when many Dutch people were close to starvation.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A plan that depends on everything going right along a single road has no margin for delay. Intelligence that contradicts a plan's optimistic assumptions must be weighed rather than discounted. Airborne troops can seize objectives but cannot hold them for long against armour without relief.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica calls the operation a failure of military intelligence redeemed to some extent by the heroism of the soldiers; the National Army Museum calls it a costly failure but a remarkable feat of arms, and the IWM one of the most controversial episodes of the war. The sources give different dates for the end of the operation, 25 or 27 September, and different loss figures. The railway strike is debated in the Netherlands: German propaganda blamed it for the shortages, while the Dutch Railway Museum attributes the famine to the shipping ban and the freezing of the rivers; whether a strike called “by superior order”, with wages paid throughout, was an act of resistance has always been disputed. The Neue Deutsche Biographie's article on Model does not mention Arnhem, so the German side of the battle itself still rests on Britannica's account of Model's response.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the plan, the problems of landing zones, radios, weather and intelligence, and the outcome. Raymond K. Bluhm's Britannica article gives Montgomery's persuasion of Eisenhower, the course of the battle at each bridge and Model's response. The Imperial War Museums give Montgomery's aims and the fate of the airborne troops at Arnhem. Dermot Bradley's article on Model in the Neue Deutsche Biographie, in German, gives the German recovery in the west in September 1944. The Dutch Railway Museum gives the railway strike called in support of the operation, the German response and the road to the famine.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the autumn of 1944 the Japanese had been driven from many outposts in the south-west and central Pacific, and American and British naval power had grown enormously. The Allied offensive of 1944 was to culminate in an invasion of the Philippines.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The invasion aimed to cut Japan's supply lines to the East Indies and win bases for further operations. King, Nimitz and Marshall had favoured other routes, but General Douglas MacArthur, determined to return to the Philippines, prevailed. The assault on Leyte joined the central Pacific advance under Admiral Chester Nimitz and the south-west Pacific advance under MacArthur.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Japanese responded with Sho-Go, the Victory Operation: a decoy force of carriers would draw Admiral William Halsey's Third Fleet north, while three surface forces converged on Leyte Gulf to destroy the landing. Kurita told his interrogators in 1945 that his mission was to destroy the landing forces at daybreak on 25 October; Ozawa said the decoy was basically Admiral Toyoda's idea and that he expected his fleet to be destroyed. The Americans aimed to protect the landing and, in Halsey's orders, to destroy the major part of the Japanese fleet if the chance arose.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Leyte, in the central Philippines, had an undefended approach from the east and good anchorages. The Japanese central force had to pass through the Sibuyan Sea and the San Bernardino Strait north of Samar; the southern forces through the Surigao Strait. The battle was fought in several widely separated engagements.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: MacArthur had overall command of the Leyte operation; Vice Admiral Thomas Kinkaid's Seventh Fleet, his principal naval force, supported the landings, while Halsey's Third Fleet, with the fast carriers and battleships, reported to Nimitz. No single commander controlled both fleets. On the Japanese side Vice Admiral Kurita Takeo led the central force with the battleships Yamato and Musashi, Vice Admirals Nishimura Shōji and Shima Kiyohide the southern forces, and Vice Admiral Ozawa Jisaburō the decoy carriers, which had few aircraft: Ozawa said many of his carrier aircraft had been sent to Formosa on Toyoda's orders. The Japanese forces were coordinated only through Toyoda, by radio.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 20 October American troops landed on the east coast of Leyte almost unopposed, and MacArthur waded ashore. The Japanese had chosen to defend farther inland. Their fleet was already moving under Sho-Go.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 23 October American submarines found Kurita's force off Palawan and sank two heavy cruisers, including his flagship. On 24 October Third Fleet aircraft sank the battleship Musashi in the Sibuyan Sea, while a Japanese bomb set the light carrier Princeton ablaze; Kurita turned west, then resumed his course. That night Nishimura's force was annihilated in the Surigao Strait by the battleships and cruisers of the Seventh Fleet and an Australian task force, and Shima turned back. Halsey, sighting Ozawa's carriers, took the whole Third Fleet north. At dawn on 25 October Kurita's battleships came out of the San Bernardino Strait off Samar and met Taffy 3, a group of escort carriers, destroyers and destroyer escorts, which fought back so fiercely, with aircraft from other task groups, that Kurita broke off and withdrew. Off Cape Engaño Halsey's aircraft sank all four of Ozawa's carriers. On 25 October the first kamikaze attack sank an escort carrier.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Halsey's decision to take the whole Third Fleet north after Ozawa's decoy, without leaving a force to guard the San Bernardino Strait, left the landing area exposed; Nimitz's signal asking where Task Force 34 was, with its padding misread as a rebuke, finally turned him back. Kurita's decision to withdraw off Samar, when he was close to the transports, saved the Seventh Fleet. Kurita told his interrogators that he expected heavy air attack inside the Gulf and judged that he could do no good there, so he turned north to join Ozawa against the American carriers; fuel, he said, was no consideration in that choice, though it governed his later withdrawal. Ozawa accepted that his force was meant to be sacrificed; he had little confidence in the lure and put its chances at even.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The destruction of the southern force at Surigao Strait, the resistance of Taffy 3 off Samar and Kurita's withdrawal decided the battle: Sho-Go failed to reach the landing area. Japanese communications failed at the decisive moment: according to an officer from Ozawa's flagship, questioned with Kurita, the reports Ozawa sent on 24 October never reached Kurita, who therefore did not know that the decoy had worked, while Ozawa believed it was failing.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Sho-Go failed to disrupt the Leyte landings and cost Japan most of what remained of its fleet, including four carriers and the battleship Musashi. The National WWII Museum calls the result a decisive American victory that ended the Japanese navy as a strategic force; Britannica writes that it crippled the Combined Fleet and reinforced Allied control of the Pacific.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: MacArthur's campaign went on to Luzon and Manila, and the way opened to Okinawa. Organised kamikaze attacks, first met off Samar, killed thousands of Allied personnel in the remaining months of the war.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Divided command over forces fighting the same battle invites failure; at Leyte the lack of a single commander over Halsey and Kinkaid nearly cost the landing. Ambiguous orders and signals shape decisions as much as the enemy does. A fleet without air cover is helpless, as Samuel Eliot Morison concluded from the battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Halsey's decision has been debated from the moment it was made; the National WWII Museum lists his ambiguous orders, his wish to sink carriers, his belief that Kurita was retreating and poor intelligence on Japanese air losses. Kurita's reasons for withdrawing are also disputed: he may have taken the escort carriers for fleet carriers, could not know that the decoy had worked, and later said he feared air attack in the gulf; some officers called him a coward. His own account, given to American interrogators in October 1945, stresses the air threat and his judgment that he could not be effective in the Gulf, and plays down fuel; it should be read as testimony given to the victors after the war.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the strategic setting, the landings, Sho-Go and each engagement in detail, with Nimitz's signal and its aftermath. The National WWII Museum gives the command arrangements, the Japanese plan, the course of the battle and the debates over Halsey's and Kurita's decisions. The U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey's interrogations of Kurita and Ozawa in Tokyo in October 1945 give the two Japanese commanders' own accounts of their missions and decisions.
