sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the breakout from Normandy the Allies crossed France into Belgium, but their advance lost momentum in the autumn of 1944, apart from the failed thrust to Arnhem. Some Allied leaders predicted that the war would end by Christmas, while the German defence was strengthened with reserves and new forces.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Hitler saw a last chance in the west. He hoped a decisive blow would split the Western Allies and lead to a negotiated peace that would let him concentrate on the Eastern Front. LeMO dates German planning for a relieving counter-offensive to the late summer of 1944, in answer to the unstoppable Allied advance in France; by separating the British and American armies the Western Powers were to be made ready for peace, so that the forces could then be turned against the Red Army. The Bundesarchiv puts the aim as splitting the Allied armies, cutting their supply lines and forcing peace negotiations.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The German offensive, code-named “Wacht am Rhein” (Watch on the Rhine), was to break through the American front in the Ardennes, cross the Meuse and drive to Antwerp, cutting off the British army group from the Americans and from its supplies. Both German sources note that it was modelled on the “Sichelschnitt” advance through the same wooded hills in May 1940; LeMO names Brussels and Antwerp, where Allied supplies were handled, as its goals. The Fifth Panzer Army was to wheel north-west past Namur to Antwerp, and the Sixth Panzer Army to thrust past Liège.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Ardennes in Belgium and Luxembourg is hilly and wooded country, regarded as difficult for a large offensive. The woods concealed the German concentration, but deep valleys turned the through roads into bottlenecks, which made road junctions such as St Vith and Bastogne vital. Winter weather at first grounded Allied aircraft.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt had overall command of the offensive; the Fifth Panzer Army was led by Hasso von Manteuffel and the Sixth Panzer Army by Sepp Dietrich. The attack was carried out by Army Group B under Field Marshal Walter Model, and a Bundesarchiv photograph shows Model, Rundstedt and Hans Krebs at a preliminary meeting in November 1944; according to the Neue Deutsche Biographie, Model played a leading part in planning and conducting the offensive. The Bundesarchiv adds that the Germans were far superior in numbers in the sector and that the American Shermans had little to set against German Tiger and Panther tanks. General Dwight D. Eisenhower, the Supreme Allied Commander, held a front of nearly 1,000 kilometres; in the Ardennes the Allied troops were mainly American, some new and inexperienced, others exhausted.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Germans massed their forces in secret, moving at night and under radio silence, and timed the attack for weather that would keep Allied aircraft on the ground. By mid-December, LeMO writes, the Wehrmacht had brought fresh infantry divisions into position between Monschau and Echternach, some withdrawn from the Eastern Front, facing relatively weak American forces. The Bundesarchiv says Hitler deliberately chose the date to deprive the Allies of their air superiority. Records of the preparations, including a map of the operation, survive in the Bundesarchiv (holding RH 19-IV).

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The offensive began before dawn on 16 December 1944 and achieved complete surprise, pushing a bulge into the American line. Small American units delayed the spearhead; in the north, LeMO notes, the Sixth SS Panzer Army advanced comparatively slowly, while the Fifth Panzer Army in the south drove quickly toward the Meuse. On 17 December soldiers of Kampfgruppe Peiper, of the 1st SS Panzer Division Leibstandarte SS Adolf Hitler, murdered American prisoners near Malmedy, and in the following days soldiers of the same division murdered civilians at Stavelot. The defenders of St Vith held the crossroads for nearly a week, until it fell on 21 December, and Bastogne, surrounded, was held by the 101st Airborne Division; on 22 December its commander, Anthony McAuliffe, answered a demand for surrender with “NUTS!”. By 24 December the Fifth Panzer Army was within about 6 kilometres of the Meuse, but fuel shortages and growing air attacks stopped it. Patton's Third Army relieved Bastogne on 26 December, and on 27 December, LeMO writes, the Wehrmacht had to go over to the defensive on every sector. The weather cleared and Allied air attacks resumed; on 1 January the Luftwaffe struck Allied airfields but suffered losses it could not recover from. The First Army counter-attacked on 3 January, and by the end of January the Allies had regained their former positions.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Montgomery, who took charge on the northern flank, swung his reserves south to forestall the Germans at the Meuse crossings, and Patton's Third Army broke through to relieve Bastogne. The quick arrival of Allied reinforcements and the decision to hold the road junctions at St Vith and Bastogne, even when surrounded, slowed the German advance. The Germans then carried out a skilful withdrawal from the potential trap. On the German side, Hitler chose the timing for bad weather, and Model, according to the Neue Deutsche Biographie, finally agreed to Hitler's “Große Lösung” (grand solution); the same article judges him an optimist inclined to ignore difficulties.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The stands at St Vith, Bastogne and on the northern shoulder denied the Germans the roads they needed, and by the end of December, short of fuel and under renewed air attack, their advance had ground to a halt. The German sources give the same reasons: the arrival of American reinforcements, better flying weather for Allied aircraft and the failure of supplies, while lack of fuel, heavy snow and difficult ground kept the heavy tanks from being used, so that the Germans lost a decisive advantage.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Allied line bulged but did not break. Germany lost men and material it could not replace, and Britannica judges that while the offensive upset Allied preparations, it forfeited any chance of prolonged German resistance. Churchill called it undoubtedly the greatest American battle of the war, and it was one of the bloodiest.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Germany had drained its last reserves of manpower and material in the west. The Bundesarchiv calls it the last great German offensive on the Western Front and notes that its failure ended Hitler's plan to end the war in the west and relieve the Eastern Front: the Americans and British advanced eastward, and the Red Army reached the Oder at the end of January. The Allies resumed their advance and in early spring crossed into the heart of Germany. The murder of American prisoners near Malmedy was one of the most brutal war crimes against American troops in Europe; Joachim Peiper was sentenced to death by a US military court in 1946, but the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment in 1951 and he was released in 1956.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Complacency and confidence that the enemy is beaten invite surprise. Holding road junctions in difficult country can stop an offensive that depends on speed and captured fuel. Rapid regrouping of reserves and decisive commanders turned a crisis into a defeat for the attacker.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the end of the battle to 16 January (Britannica) or 25 January 1945 (the National WWII Museum, the IWM); LeMO says the Germans had lost all their gains by 16 January, and the Bundesarchiv that the offensive had wholly failed by the end of January. Britannica credits Montgomery's swing of reserves to the Meuse with frustrating the German advance; the brief's controversy over his press conference is not discussed in the sources read. Britannica judges the offensive profitable in its own terms but fatal in relation to the whole war. Britannica gives Rundstedt overall command, while the Bundesarchiv and the Neue Deutsche Biographie put Model at the centre of the planning and conduct. The Neue Deutsche Biographie writes that the Allies stopped the attack only after a week, LeMO that it failed after only a few days. The German sources' figures for the forces engaged are not used.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the German plan, the commanders, the course of the battle and its assessment. The National WWII Museum gives Hitler's aims, the German preparations, the delaying actions, the Malmedy massacre and the defence of St Vith and Bastogne. The IWM gives the surprise, the role of the road junctions, the weather and fuel, and the outcome. The Bundesarchiv's article, LeMO's article and Dermot Bradley's article on Model in the Neue Deutsche Biographie, all in German, give the German aims and plan, Model's part, the war crimes at Malmedy and Stavelot and Peiper's trial, and the German view of why the offensive failed.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The American counteroffensive in the Pacific was divided between MacArthur, advancing through New Guinea to the Philippines, and Admiral Chester Nimitz, advancing across the central Pacific. By October 1944 MacArthur had landed in the Philippines and Nimitz had taken the Mariana Islands, from which B-29 bombers could strike Japan.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: General Henry Arnold of the Army Air Forces wanted Iwo Jima, halfway between the Marianas and Tokyo, as a base for fighters to escort the bombers. Nimitz, on his admirals' advice, proposed taking Iwo Jima and Okinawa rather than Formosa, and the Joint Chiefs approved. The island was part of the Tokyo prefecture, Japanese home soil, and had a civilian population; most of the islanders were forcibly evacuated to the mainland in 1944, but some were ordered to stay, and not a few of them died in the fighting.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Operation Detachment aimed to take the island and its airfields. The Japanese aimed to inflict such heavy losses that the Americans might be deterred from invading the home islands.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Iwo Jima is a small volcanic island, about 8 kilometres long, about 1,220 kilometres from Tokyo, dotted with caves and covered with volcanic sand and ash. Mount Suribachi, at its south-western tip, overlooks most of the island; two airfields lay in the middle and a third, unfinished, to the north. The landing beaches were backed by steep terraces of volcanic ash.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Lieutenant General Kuribayashi Tadamichi, appointed to command the 109th Division, responsible for the defence of the Bonin area, on 27 May 1944, arrived on Iwo Jima on 8 June. He had his garrison build a network of tunnels and hundreds of pillboxes, blockhouses and gun positions. Rather than defend the beaches heavily, he kept his men underground until the Americans had advanced inland, and ordered them not to make banzai charges. Nimitz formed a joint expeditionary force; Major General Harry Schmidt led the Marine landing force of three Marine divisions. US intelligence underestimated the garrison.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Marines' commander asked for ten days of naval bombardment but was given three because of the schedule for Okinawa; poor weather and the buried defences meant it did little damage. The Marines were to land on the south-eastern beaches, cut across the island to isolate Suribachi and drive north past the airfields.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At about 9 a.m. on 19 February 1945 the Marines landed. The ash terraces slowed them and the beaches became congested under Japanese fire, but by evening Suribachi was cut off. On 21 February kamikaze aircraft damaged several American ships. Marines took Suribachi on 23 February and twice raised a flag on its summit; Joe Rosenthal's photograph of the second raising became one of the war's most famous images. The Marines then fought north yard by yard, taking the airfields and fighting for weeks at places they called the Meat Grinder and the Amphitheater, using flamethrowers against caves and bunkers. On 8 March a Japanese naval officer led a banzai attack against Kuribayashi's orders. The island was declared secure on 16 March, but the last major engagement was a night attack on 26 March.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Kuribayashi's decision to give up the beaches and fight from tunnels and caves, and to forbid banzai charges, made the Marines pay for every position. On the American side, the decision to shorten the bombardment to keep to the Okinawa schedule, and an underestimate of the garrison, made the landing costlier.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The capture of Suribachi on 23 February and the breakthrough of the central Japanese line at the end of February decided the battle, but the defenders fought on in the north for weeks. On the night of 7 March Kuribayashi telegraphed the deputy chief of the Army General Staff that the greatest difficulty of the defence had been an island almost entirely flat, without natural strongpoints, whose airfields eased the enemy's advance, and that still more fatal was a gap in material so great that no tactics or countermeasures could make up for it.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The United States took Iwo Jima at a cost among the heaviest in the history of the Marine Corps. Almost the entire Japanese garrison was killed; only a few hundred were taken prisoner, and Kuribayashi himself did not surrender. Twenty-seven Medals of Honor were awarded, fourteen of them posthumously.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The island's airfields were used for the rest of the war, and B-29s landed there. The National WWII Museum notes that the bloodbath horrified Allied planners and the public, who feared an even greater slaughter in an invasion of Japan. The flag-raising photograph became a symbol, reproduced on posters and a stamp and in the Marine Corps War Memorial. After the war the island was used by the American forces and then Japan's Self-Defense Forces, and half a century after its return to Japan its former inhabitants have still not been allowed to go home.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A defence in depth, dug in against overwhelming firepower, can make the cost of an objective very high even when defeat is certain. An objective's value must be weighed against that cost before the attack, not justified afterwards.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Whether the island was worth its cost is debated. Britannica cites the historian Robert Burrell's finding that the fighter escort missions that were the main reason for the invasion were few, that most B-29 landings were not strictly emergencies, and that the Joint Chiefs did not consider the Marines' doubts. The sources date the end of the battle to 16 or 26 March; the Japanese National Institute for Defense Studies counts 36 days, from the landing on 19 February to the final collapse of the Japanese defence on 26 March. The National WWII Museum describes the long confusion over whether the flag-raising photograph was staged.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Myles Hudson's Britannica article gives the strategic background, Kuribayashi's defence, the course of the battle and the debate over its cost. The National WWII Museum's article on Iwo Jima and Okinawa gives the defence and the fighting, and Keith Huxen's 75th-anniversary article gives the flag-raising and its legacy. The National Institute for Defense Studies of Japan's Ministry of Defense, in Japanese, introduces Kuribayashi's papers, including his telegram of 7 March 1945; Meiji Gakuin University's notice of a lecture by Ishihara Shun, in Japanese, gives the fate of the island's civilians.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: As the battle for Iwo Jima ended in March 1945, American commanders prepared Operation Iceberg, the invasion of Okinawa. American planners expected the losses of Iwo Jima to be repeated on a much greater scale, and hoped to overwhelm the defenders with a massive bombardment and the largest amphibious landing of the Pacific War.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Okinawa, the largest of the Ryukyu Islands, lies about 563 kilometres south of Kyushu, and its capture was regarded as a vital precursor to a ground invasion of the Japanese home islands. It was the last island battle before that anticipated invasion.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Americans aimed to take the island as a springboard for the invasion of Japan. The Japanese aimed to make the cost as high as possible, on land from prepared positions in the south and at sea with mass suicide attacks on the fleet.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Okinawa is about 100 kilometres long and at most 32 kilometres wide. Its southern part, around Naha and Shuri, was heavily fortified along high ridges, with Shuri Castle as the keystone, and its many caves gave the defenders shelter from bombardment. The island had a large civilian population, which the Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum describes as fully mobilized for the battle, the only ground battle fought on Japanese soil. Heavy rain and rugged terrain slowed the fighting.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Under the overall command of Admiral Chester Nimitz, Admiral Raymond Spruance's Fifth Fleet oversaw the landings and Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. commanded the US Tenth Army of Army and Marine divisions. Lieutenant General Ushijima Mitsuru commanded the Japanese garrison, which had thoroughly fortified the island. Japan retained enough aircraft for mass suicide attacks.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Air and sea attacks began as early as October 1944, and in March 1945 the carriers of Task Force 58 destroyed hundreds of Japanese aircraft. On 26 March American troops landed on the Kerama Islands to the west, where they found boats assembled for suicide attacks, and artillery was placed on the islets of Keise to support the main landing.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 1 April the Tenth Army landed at Hagushi on the west coast, almost unopposed, and by 4 April had cut the island in two. On 6–7 April the Japanese struck the fleet with hundreds of kamikaze aircraft and sent the battleship Yamato on a sortie without air cover; carrier aircraft sank it on 7 April. The north of the island was cleared by 22 April. In the south the Americans met the fortified line through Naha, Shuri and Yonabaru, where the fighting was positional and savage: flame-throwing tanks led infantry against caves that had to be destroyed one by one, and the Japanese neither took prisoners nor generally surrendered. American troops entered Naha's suburbs on 12 May. Shuri fell at the turn of May and June, and the Naha airfield was taken in early June. Buckner was killed by artillery fire on 18 June while visiting a forward post, and major combat operations ended on 21 June. On 22 June Ushijima and his chief of staff killed themselves rather than surrender.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Ushijima's decision not to contest the beaches but to hold the fortified south, using caves and ridges, forced the Americans into costly frontal assaults: the Americans advanced only about 6 kilometres in the south between early April and late May. When Shuri could no longer be held, the army withdrew to the southern tip rather than fight a decisive battle there; the museum describes this as a choice to wage a bloody war of attrition, in the area where civilians had taken refuge. The Japanese command's reliance on mass suicide attacks at sea made the battle as costly for the navy as for the army. American commanders relied on the quantity and quality of their equipment, advancing in waves by day under heavy artillery support.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The battle for the Shuri line, from late April to the end of May, decided the campaign. Once Shuri fell, the defenders were exhausted and confined to the southern tip; Britannica notes that the Japanese lost Okinawa because they ran out of caves and boulders from which to fight and men to do the fighting.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The United States took Okinawa, at an enormous price on both sides. Both commanding generals died. Very few Japanese soldiers surrendered. The kamikaze attacks sank most of the American ships lost in the battle, and the navy suffered heavily.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The civilian population of Okinawa suffered catastrophically: Britannica writes that it was reduced by perhaps a quarter, with men, women and children killed in the fighting or ordered by the Japanese military to commit suicide, in some cases with a grenade given to a family to detonate when capture seemed near. The Peace Memorial Museum writes that civilian deaths far exceeded military ones: civilians were killed by shelling, starvation and malaria, by suicide, and by retreating Japanese troops, and in some caves Japanese soldiers killed civilians or forced them into mass suicide. The savagery of the battle shaped American expectations of an invasion of the home islands, which planners now expected to be terribly costly.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A defence in depth, from caves and ridges, can make every advance costly even against overwhelming firepower. Attrition at sea from suicide attacks can match the cost of the land battle. A battle fought among a civilian population makes civilians among its principal victims, and a military that orders civilians to die rather than surrender multiplies the catastrophe.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources give different figures for civilian deaths and military losses, and date the end of the battle to 21 or 22 June. Britannica records that American naval officers at first understated the effectiveness of the kamikaze attacks. The National WWII Museum and Britannica both link the battle's cost to American planning for the invasion of Japan, while the Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum presents the battle from the perspective of Okinawans, as a “Typhoon of Steel” in which the Japanese army's conduct was itself a cause of civilian deaths.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the planning, the commanders, the course of the battle, the kamikaze campaign, the civilian deaths and the battle's significance for the invasion of Japan. The National WWII Museum gives the purpose of the battle, the landing, the Shuri line, the kamikaze attacks, Buckner's death and the civilian toll. The Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum's English guide and exhibit text give the Okinawan civilians' experience; its figures are not used.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In January 1945 the Red Army broke out of its bridgeheads on the Vistula, took Warsaw and advanced to the Oder, where by early February it stood about 65 kilometres from Berlin. German civilians fled west in their millions, joined by concentration camp prisoners forced on death marches, many of whom died. Stalin then halted the advance, and the Soviets cleared their flanks in Pomerania and Silesia.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Stalin mistrusted the Western Allies and wanted to take Berlin first; LeMO calls the capture of the German capital the declared aim of the Soviet leadership. When the Western Allies crossed the Rhine and approached the city in early April, he accelerated the attack. Hitler and committed Nazis had no option but to fight on, and many German soldiers fought in fear of what the Soviets would do in Germany after what German forces had done in the Soviet Union.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Soviet aim was to take Berlin and end the war. The main thrust was divided between Marshal Georgy Zhukov's 1st Belorussian Front and Marshal Ivan Konev's 1st Ukrainian Front, in what became a race for the city. The high command's directive gave Berlin to Zhukov's front, but both marshals recall Stalin cutting short the boundary between the fronts at Lübben, south-east of the city; Zhukov writes that Stalin told Konev to be ready to strike at Berlin from the south if Zhukov was held up. The Germans aimed only to prolong the war.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Seelow Heights west of the Oder were the only place where the Germans had any hope of stopping the Soviets, and were fortified; beyond them there was little between the Soviets and Berlin. The city, repeatedly bombed, had few fixed defences, but its ruined streets favoured the defenders and made the final advance slow.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Soviets massed one of the largest concentrations of military power ever seen, with Zhukov's and Konev's fronts joined by Marshal Konstantin Rokossovsky's 2nd Belorussian Front in the north. The German defenders were shattered formations, stragglers and the Volkssturm militia of teenagers and old men, with Hitler Youth units, armed with the Panzerfaust; LeMO adds Waffen-SS units and improvised police formations, short of ammunition and fuel. A defender's account describes one sector held by a scratch force of interpreters, Volkssturm, alert units and police, short of automatic weapons.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: German intelligence had detected the Soviet build-up, but Hitler refused to believe the reports. The Germans withdrew their defenders from the first line of trenches at the Seelow Heights just before the Soviet barrage; Zhukov writes that reconnaissance in force on 14 and 15 April had led them to bring reserves up to their second positions. To the south, Konev chose a long barrage in darkness, without searchlights, to hide his crossing of the Neisse.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 16 April Zhukov's front attacked at the Seelow Heights. The barrage fell on empty trenches, and searchlights meant to blind the defenders silhouetted the attackers; Zhukov sent in his tanks before a breakthrough had been made, and they struggled on churned ground. Konev's attack further south succeeded, and on the night of 17 April his tank armies were turned north toward Berlin. Zhukov's troops took the heights on the morning of 18 April, and on the fourth day the German line at Seelow broke. On 20 April Rokossovsky joined the attack and Soviet shells began to fall on the city. Hitler forbade retreat and ordered attacks by units that scarcely existed. By 25 April Berlin was encircled by Konev's and Zhukov's fronts. The Red Army fought through the city house by house, demolishing buildings that held defenders. Hitler killed himself on 30 April, after learning that the last relief attempt, by Wenck's Twelfth Army, had been broken off near Potsdam; that day a Soviet banner flew on the Reichstag, which French volunteers of the Waffen-SS had helped defend. On 2 May the garrison surrendered; Germany capitulated at Reims on 7 May and in Berlin-Karlshorst the next day.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Stalin's decision to split the attack between Zhukov and Konev manufactured a race for Berlin; he taunted Zhukov with giving the city to Konev, and later gave Zhukov the honour of taking the Reichstag. Britannica writes that both marshals were willing to accept enormous casualties and inflict colossal damage, and that Stalin's fixation on the symbolic Reichstag cost many Soviet lives. Zhukov's decision to send in his tanks before a breakthrough added to his losses. In his own account, he had planned the night attack with searchlights and meant to hold his tank armies back until the heights fell, but at about 13:00 on 16 April, seeing the defence largely intact, he committed both; that evening Stalin told him he should not have committed the 1st Guards Tank Army there and ordered Konev's tank armies toward Berlin. Hitler's refusal to allow retreat let the German Ninth Army be encircled.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The breaking of the Seelow Heights on the fourth day of the battle opened the road to Berlin, and the encirclement of the city on 25 April sealed its fate.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Berlin fell to the Red Army, and with it the Third Reich; the general surrender of German forces followed within a week. Losses on all sides were very heavy, and the city lay in ruins.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: German civilians and refugees trapped in the city suffered terribly: boys were sent to the front, civilians caught deserting were executed, and Soviet fire took no account of civilian lives. LeMO describes some two million inhabitants sheltering in cellars and bunkers, and SS squads shooting civilians and soldiers suspected of weakening resistance under a Führer order of 22 April. Soviet soldiers committed rape and sexual violence against German women on a vast scale; the IWM describes it as effectively state-sanctioned. The Soviet victory, the IWM notes, came from the greatest mass mobilisation in history and the immense sacrifice of the Soviet people.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Political goals, the race for Berlin and the symbolic Reichstag, can override military economy and multiply the cost of an operation. Urban assault against even scratch defenders is slow and destructive. A war waged as a war of annihilation ends in vengeance on the attacker's own civilians.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the battle from 16 April (the IWM and LeMO, counting the Seelow Heights) or from 20 April (Britannica, counting the fighting for the city). They give different figures for the forces and for military and civilian losses, which the IWM notes are almost impossible to calculate for civilians. The IWM discusses why German soldiers fought to the end; Klaus Sommer's account, set down after the war, shows defenders clinging to official promises of relief armies until the last day, and those who tried to avoid the fighting treated as traitors. Britannica stresses the cost of Stalin's fixation on the Reichstag. The two marshals' memoirs, written as rivals long after the event, defend their own conduct: Zhukov admits only a "slip", an underestimate of the Seelow terrain, and insists that Konev's tank armies were turned on Berlin by the high command, not on Konev's initiative; Konev concedes that Stalin's unfinished boundary may have been meant to set the fronts competing, and admits his own wish to take the city. They place Lübben 60 and 80 kilometres from Berlin. Zhukov also writes that Rokossovsky's main forces could attack only from 24 April.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Robert Rumble's account for the Imperial War Museums gives the Vistula–Oder offensive, Stalin's decisions, the Seelow Heights, the encirclement, the street fighting, the violence against civilians and the end of the war. John Swift's Britannica article gives the forces, the race between Zhukov and Konev, the urban fighting, the suffering of civilians and the surrender. LeMO, the German Historical Museum's online history, gives the German side of the battle, and its eyewitness series the account of Klaus Sommer, born in 1927, who fought in the city as a young soldier in his father's sector; the opinions in it are his own. The Soviet side comes from the memoirs of the two front commanders, Zhukov and Konev, in the English editions published in Moscow. Their force figures are not used.

phases.title: Seelow Heights
phases.description: Zhukov attacks at the Seelow Heights and is held for days while Konev breaks through to the south.

phases.title: Toward the city
phases.description: Rokossovsky joins the attack; shells fall on Berlin; Konev and Zhukov encircle the city.

phases.title: Street fighting
phases.description: The Red Army fights house by house toward the centre; Hitler kills himself on 30 April; a banner flies on the Reichstag.

phases.description: The garrison surrenders on 2 May; Germany capitulates within a week.

perspectives.name: Georgy Zhukov
perspectives.objective: Take Berlin with the 1st Belorussian Front.
perspectives.known: The Seelow Heights were the last fortified line before the city.
perspectives.uncertainty: How long the Germans could hold Seelow; he writes that he and his staff doubted beforehand that the heights could be broken quickly.
perspectives.constraints: Stalin's pressure and the rivalry with Konev's front; Stalin reproached him for committing a tank army where the directive had not provided for it.
perspectives.decision: He attacked at night under searchlights, committed both tank armies at midday on 16 April before a breakthrough, took the heights on 18 April, then fought into the city and took the Reichstag.
perspectives.forces: The 1st Belorussian Front.
perspectives.terrain: The Seelow Heights, swampy ground and the ruined streets of Berlin.
perspectives.logistics: A massive concentration of artillery and armour on the Oder.
perspectives.outcome: His front broke through on the fourth day and took the centre of Berlin.

perspectives.name: Konstantin Rokossovsky
perspectives.objective: Join the final offensive from the north.
perspectives.known: His front had been transferred after the fall of Königsberg.
perspectives.uncertainty: How quickly he could break through in the north.
perspectives.constraints: Late arrival in the battle.
perspectives.decision: He joined the attack on 20 April and broke through in the north.
perspectives.forces: The 2nd Belorussian Front.
perspectives.terrain: The lower Oder north of Berlin.
perspectives.logistics: A front moved from East Prussia.
perspectives.outcome: German forces in the north retreated westward.

perspectives.name: Adolf Hitler
perspectives.objective: Hold Berlin and prolong the war.
perspectives.known: The Soviets were massing on the Oder; his generals called the front a house of cards.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the relief attacks he ordered could break the siege.
perspectives.constraints: Shattered formations, the Volkssturm and no fuel.
perspectives.decision: He refused to believe intelligence reports, forbade retreat, ordered attacks by forces that scarcely existed and stayed in Berlin with Goebbels and Bormann while other leaders left.
perspectives.forces: The remnants of the German armies and the city's defenders.
perspectives.terrain: The Reich Chancellery and the ruined city.
perspectives.logistics: Units without men or fuel.
perspectives.outcome: He killed himself on 30 April; the garrison surrendered on 2 May.

perspectives.name: Ivan Konev
perspectives.objective: Break through on the Neisse and, if the chance came, strike at Berlin from the south.
perspectives.known: Stalin had cut short the boundary with Zhukov's front at Lübben, leaving room for an attack on the city from the south.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his front would be allowed to turn on Berlin, since the directive assigned the city to Zhukov.
perspectives.constraints: A river to force under fire, and a boundary with Zhukov's front that Stalin could redraw at any time.
perspectives.forces: The 1st Ukrainian Front, with Rybalko's and Lelyushenko's tank armies.
perspectives.terrain: The Neisse, then open country and the southern approaches to Berlin.
perspectives.logistics: A long night barrage and the darkness itself to cover the crossing of the Neisse.
perspectives.decision: He crossed the Neisse without searchlights and, on the night of 17 April, turned his tank armies north toward Berlin.
perspectives.outcome: His tank armies fought into Berlin from the south; when the boundary between the fronts was fixed, the centre of the city fell to Zhukov's zone and Konev turned Rybalko's corps west.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In the first week of July 1940, a month after Italy entered the war, Italian forces took the Sudanese frontier posts of Kassala, Gallabat and Kurmuk. Playfair writes that by the end of August the British had lost these posts, British Somaliland and Moyale on the Kenya border, while the Patriot movement against Italian rule was gaining strength inside Ethiopia. In September the 5th Indian Division and a squadron of tanks began to reach the Sudan.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Wavell ordered step-by-step action on the Sudan front, not a general offensive. At a meeting in Khartoum beginning on 28 October, the day Italy attacked Greece, the Secretary of State for War, Anthony Eden, proposed that Gallabat should be attacked early in November and Kassala early in January. Retaking the frontier posts would open an entry into Ethiopia through which to foster the revolt. The 1942 Ministry of Information account calls Gallabat the gate of the Abyssinian rebellion and of the province of Amhara, whose capital was Gondar.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: On Wavell's instructions Major-General Heath of the 5th Indian Division planned an attack by the 10th Indian Infantry Brigade under Brigadier W. J. Slim, with a squadron of the 6th Royal Tank Regiment. In a first phase the 3rd Royal Garhwal Rifles, led by the tanks, were to take Gallabat Fort and if possible win a bridgehead over the dry river bed beyond it; in a second phase the 1st Essex were to attack Metemma. The aim, as the 1942 account puts it, was to break Metemma and open the caravan routes into Gojjam to support the Patriots.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Gallabat Fort stood on a ridge on the Sudanese side of a dry river bed with steep banks, the Boundary Khor, which marked the frontier; the post and village of Metemma lay beyond it. Clearings had been burnt round the fort for a field of fire. The ground was open, rocky and hard, with long grass that hid boulders and mines, and there was little cover from the air.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Slim's brigade combined one British and two Indian battalions, as each brigade of the 5th Indian Division then did, with field artillery and a squadron of cruiser and light tanks. Both Italian posts had good field defences: Gallabat was held by a colonial battalion and Metemma by two more colonial battalions and irregular bande, with pack artillery and anti-tank weapons. The 1942 account names the Italian commander at Gallabat–Metemma as Lieutenant-Colonel Castagnola and the commander at Gondar, who promised him air support, as General Martini. Only a few bombers, fighters and army co-operation aircraft of the Royal Air Force were available, flying from temporary strips, against Italian fighters and bombers within range of the area.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The attack was planned for 8 November, but reports at the end of October of Italian reinforcements moving up from Gondar brought it forward to 6 November. The 4th Baluch held the outpost line and stayed in reserve. The 1942 account says that the brigade assembled within a mile or two of the Italian lines without the Italian commander learning of it. Rain on the evening of 5 November made the forward landing ground unusable until mid-morning on the 6th.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Air and artillery bombardment opened at 5.30 on 6 November, and at 6.15 the Garhwalis attacked behind the tanks. The tanks failed to break the stockade, but two riflemen cut the wire and the fort was overrun by about 7.30; an Italian counter-attack towards the river bed was repulsed. By then most of the tanks were out of action. From mid-morning Italian bombers, with their fighters in command of the air, attacked the fort repeatedly; there was little cover and no anti-aircraft guns. The bombing continued on 7 November, and Slim withdrew from the fort to less exposed ground; Wavell's despatch says that artillery fire then made Metemma untenable for the Italians, though it could not be occupied. The Italians withdrew from Gallabat and Metemma towards Gondar on the night of 31 January 1941.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: With only one cruiser tank still running and the wire round Metemma intact, Slim decided on 6 November not to go on with the attack on Metemma and to consolidate the ground gained; Playfair describes the attack as postponed until the tanks could be repaired. The next day, with the tank workshop vehicle destroyed, no hope of repairs and the bombing continuing, Slim decided to evacuate Gallabat and withdraw to positions within artillery range of Metemma. Playfair places the decision in the afternoon of 7 November and the new position about three miles west of Gallabat; the withdrawal was not interfered with.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of the tanks and the loss of the air decided the action. The Indian official history names the mechanical breakdown of the tanks and Italian air superiority as the two reasons for failure; Playfair says the tanks were disabled mainly by mines and boulders in the grass, and that the British fighters, inferior to the Italian ones, were shot down early. On the afternoon of 6 November the casualties of the bombing caused confusion, and elements in the rear began to withdraw without orders before the situation was brought under control.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Gallabat was taken but not held, and Metemma was not attacked. Playfair states plainly that the operation failed of its object; Wavell's despatch calls it a minor attack and a partially successful action. The Indian official history judges the results disappointing, though losses were inflicted on the Italians.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Wavell decided in early December to keep up the pressure at Gallabat without large-scale operations there and to make Kassala the main attack. Patrolling in November and December gave the 5th Indian Division the upper hand in no man's land and led the Italians to overestimate its strength. Playfair and the 1942 account agree that the attack encouraged the Patriots, who saw Italian posts attacked with modern weapons. When the Italians withdrew at the end of January, a detachment of the 9th Indian Infantry Brigade followed them towards Gondar.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Taking an objective is not the same as being able to hold it: a position won in the open could not be kept once the enemy controlled the air and the attackers had no anti-aircraft defence. An attack that depended on a few tanks to break wire failed when the tanks broke down and there were no spares or reserves. The Indian official history draws the lesson that all forward troops needed protection against air attack.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources differ on why the tanks failed (mechanical causes, or mines and boulders), on the losses on both sides, which are not given here, and on the result: the 1942 account says the action was fought to a standstill but served its purpose, Wavell's despatch calls it partially successful, and Playfair says it failed. The 1942 account was wartime official publicity and its detail of the Italian side, including the commanders' names, is not confirmed by the other sources read. None of the sources describes the action from Italian records, and none names the unit that began to withdraw without orders.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Indian official history, written from the war diaries, gives the plan, the forces, the attack hour by hour and the decisions. Playfair's British official history gives the strategic setting, the air situation and the result. Wavell's despatch gives the commander-in-chief's view of the action and the policy that followed. The Ministry of Information's 1942 account gives a vivid narrative, with Italian names, written as wartime publicity.

phases.title: Preparation
phases.description: The attack is agreed at Khartoum and brought forward to forestall Italian reinforcements.

phases.title: The fort taken
phases.description: Bombardment, then the Garhwalis and the tanks storm Gallabat Fort; most tanks break down.

phases.title: Command of the air lost
phases.description: Italian bombers and fighters attack the fort; the attack on Metemma is abandoned.

phases.title: Withdrawal
phases.description: Slim pulls back from the fort to less exposed ground within artillery range of Metemma.

phases.title: Italian withdrawal
phases.description: The Italians leave Gallabat and Metemma for Gondar.

perspectives.name: William Slim
perspectives.objective: Take Gallabat Fort and then Metemma, opening the frontier and the routes to the Patriots.
perspectives.known: The Italian posts were fortified; reinforcements were reported on the road from Gondar; his attack on Metemma depended on tanks to break its wire.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the tanks would survive the ground and whether the few British fighters could hold off the Italian air force.
perspectives.constraints: No anti-aircraft guns, no spare tanks and hard ground that made digging in difficult.
perspectives.decision: When the tanks broke down and the air was lost, he gave up the attack on Metemma and then the fort itself, withdrawing to ground from which artillery could cover Metemma.
perspectives.forces: The 10th Indian Infantry Brigade, a squadron of cruiser and light tanks and field artillery.
perspectives.terrain: Open, rocky ground around the fort and a steep-banked river bed before Metemma.
perspectives.logistics: A single workshop vehicle and spares for the tanks, both lost in the bombing.
perspectives.outcome: The fort was taken and given up; the operation failed of its object.

perspectives.name: Lieutenant-Colonel Castagnola
perspectives.objective: Hold Gallabat and Metemma, the Italian posts on the road to Gondar.
perspectives.known: According to the 1942 British account, he had no warning of the attack; when Gallabat was overrun he still held Metemma and its wire.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether reinforcements from Gondar would arrive in time.
perspectives.constraints: Colonial battalions with limited artillery; the fort at Gallabat lay on open ground under British artillery fire.
perspectives.decision: He called on Gondar for reinforcements and air action, and General Martini sent bombers and fighters that attacked the fort for two days.
perspectives.forces: Colonial battalions and irregular bande, with pack artillery and anti-tank weapons.
perspectives.terrain: Fortified posts on either side of the frontier river bed.
perspectives.logistics: Air support from Gondar and reinforcements on the road behind Metemma.
perspectives.outcome: Metemma held, and the British withdrew from Gallabat; the posts were given up only in the general withdrawal at the end of January 1941.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After invading southern Burma, the Japanese Fifteenth Army occupied Rangoon on 8 March 1942; the weekly Shashin Shuho put its troops entering the city on the cover of its issue of 1 April. Kirby describes the first air raids on Rangoon in December 1941 as starting a general exodus: the city's large Indian population set out to reach India overland. Alexander, who arrived to command the Army in Burma on 5 March, asked India for a corps commander, and Lieutenant-General W. J. Slim took command of the new Burma Corps on 19 March.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: After Rangoon the defence was meant to cover the road to China, the new base around Mandalay and the oilfields at Yenangyaung, on which the Allied forces depended for fuel. Chinese armies under Stilwell held the Sittang valley, but Kirby writes that Chiang Kai-shek was never prepared to commit them wholeheartedly to Burma, and Newell that he distrusted British motives and would fight there only long enough to keep the supply line open. The Japanese, with more divisions than the Allies had estimated, planned to advance north on three axes and fight the decisive battle for Mandalay by the middle of May. Kirby judges that most Burmese were neither pro-British nor pro-Japanese, though many helped the invader once he seemed to be winning; Newell writes that sympathetic Burmese gave the Japanese detailed information on Allied movements.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Burma Corps was to hold the Irrawaddy valley and the oilfields while the Chinese held the Sittang valley, the two fronts separated by the Pegu Yomas. When central Burma could no longer be held, Alexander decided, and told Slim on 26 April, that his main object must be the defence of India: as much of the army as possible was to be brought out for reorganization, keeping touch with the Chinese and a position from which to re-enter Burma.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Irrawaddy valley north of Prome was dry and very hot in April; water was scarce, and the chaungs, stream beds running down to the river, gave the defensive lines; the Pin Chaung, north of Yenangyaung, had a single ford usable by wheeled traffic. North of Mandalay the only route for the army was a narrow sandy track from Yeu to Shwegyin on the Chindwin, through innumerable chaungs and over flimsy bridges, and from there by river steamer to Kalewa and on through the malarial Kabaw valley to Tamu. The monsoon, due in mid-May, would turn the tracks to quagmires.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Burma Corps comprised the 1st Burma Division under Bruce Scott, the 17th Indian Division under Cowan and the 7th Armoured Brigade; its staff and signals had to be found in Burma and it was never fully staffed. Stilwell commanded the Chinese Fifth and Sixth Armies under the Generalissimo's restrictions, and Lieutenant-General Sun Li-jen's 38th Division was placed under Slim's command in April. Iida's Fifteenth Army had four divisions. After the Japanese destroyed many Allied aircraft at Magwe on 22 March, the remaining air forces left Burma, and the Japanese had the air almost to themselves.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 19 March the corps was gathering in the Irrawaddy valley around Prome, with the 1st Burma Division coming across from the Sittang after relief by the Chinese 200th Division. The Chinese 200th Division held Toungoo, in the Sittang valley, unsupported; Newell calls its stand the longest defensive action of any Allied force in the campaign. Japanese road blocks and the action at Shwedaung at the end of March made Prome untenable, and on 1 April Alexander, with Wavell's approval, ordered Burma Corps back to the Allanmyo area.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: In April the corps fell back up the Irrawaddy towards Magwe while the Japanese 33rd Division worked round its flanks. On 15 April Slim gave the signal to destroy the Yenangyaung oilfields. A Japanese regiment, moving unobserved, blocked the Pin Chaung ford behind the 1st Burma Division, which fought for two days in great heat without water; on 19 April it broke out to the east, abandoning its vehicles and guns, while the Chinese 38th Division attacked from the north too late to help. Lashio fell on 29 April, closing the Burma Road. Burma Corps crossed the Irrawaddy at the Ava bridge, fought at Monywa at the beginning of May, and raced the Japanese and the monsoon to the Shwegyin ferry, where the rearguard fought its last action on 10 May. The first heavy rains fell on 12 May; the rearguards reached Tamu by 19 May, and on 20 May IV Corps took command of the troops from Burma.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Slim delayed the demolition of the oilfields until 15 April because the Allied armies needed petrol until the last moment. He told Bruce Scott to hold on the Yin Chaung to give the Chinese time to strike, and when the 1st Burma Division was cut off he refused Bruce Scott's request to abandon his transport and break out, because the Chinese were to attack at dawn. Kirby records that a false report of Japanese in Kyaukpadaung led corps headquarters to recall troops that had crossed the Pin Chaung, losing the last chance of opening the road. In the withdrawal Slim sent the whole of the 2nd Burma Brigade up the Myittha valley to block a Japanese thrust, a change Alexander confirmed on 28 April. Alexander was determined not to abandon the wounded or the refugees on the Yeu–Shwegyin track; at Shwegyin, with too few steamers, the guns, tanks and nearly all the vehicles were destroyed.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of the air at Magwe left the army without reconnaissance or cover. The loss of Toungoo opened the road into the Shan States and to Lashio, so that the whole Allied defence could be turned; Kirby calls Toungoo the key to it. The Yenangyaung action cost the 1st Burma Division much of its strength and its irreplaceable transport and guns. Alexander's decision of 25 April to retreat across the Irrawaddy, and of 26 April to make the defence of India his main object, turned the campaign into a race for the Chindwin.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Burma was lost and China's land route was cut. Kirby writes that the Army in Burma retreated nearly a thousand miles in some three and a half months without once losing its cohesion, the longest retreat ever carried out by a British army, but that very little of its armament and equipment was brought out. Wavell's despatch names Slim, Cowan and Bruce Scott as good and resolute commanders to whose efforts it was largely due that the final withdrawal was so skilfully conducted. Stilwell, Newell records, said that they had been run out of Burma and ought to find out why and go back.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The troops reached India exhausted, and dysentery and malaria took a heavy toll in the Kabaw valley; Kirby judges that another week east of the Chindwin might have led to complete disaster. Part of the Chinese force went back to China, but three divisions went west into India, where Stilwell began to prepare training bases. The Indian exodus left Burma without the labour and staff that had run its public services, and India had to become the base for any return.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An army can lose a campaign and keep its cohesion if its commanders keep it fighting, keep it supplied on the way and accept the loss of what it cannot carry; but cohesion was bought with the abandonment of guns, tanks and transport, and the retreat's cost fell hardest on those who could not keep up. A coalition whose partners have different aims cannot fight one plan, and an army without air cover and with weak intelligence will be outflanked by an enemy who moves unobserved.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources differ on small and large points. Romanus and Sunderland date the start of the oilfield demolitions to 1 a.m. on 15 April, Kirby to Slim's signal at 1 p.m. that day. Kirby explains the late Chinese attack at the Pin Chaung by delays; Romanus and Sunderland say Sun refused to attack again on 18 April without further reconnaissance. Alexander's report holds that an army's needs must come before those of refugees, but that the Indian population, which felt it must get out or be murdered, had to be evacuated if the public services were not to break down; no source read records the refugees' own experience of the march, and their losses are not given here. The casualty figures in Kirby are also left out. The Japanese side is told here mostly through Kirby's use of Japanese records; the Japanese army's own monograph on this phase was not readable.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Kirby's British official history gives the narrative, the Japanese plans from their records and the review of the campaign. Wavell's despatch carries Hutton's and Alexander's reports, with their views on the Chinese, the refugees and the commanders. Romanus and Sunderland give the American and Chinese side at Yenangyaung, and Newell's brochure the theatre, the Chinese command and Stilwell's walk out. The JACAR timeline gives the Japanese wartime record of Rangoon's fall.

phases.title: Prome
phases.description: Slim takes command of Burma Corps; Toungoo falls and the corps leaves Prome.

phases.title: Yenangyaung
phases.description: The oilfields are destroyed; the 1st Burma Division is cut off and breaks out as the Chinese attack.

phases.title: Across the Irrawaddy
phases.description: Alexander orders the retreat to India; Burma Corps crosses at Ava and fights at Monywa.

phases.title: Shwegyin
phases.description: The race for the Chindwin ferry; the rearguard's last action; guns and vehicles destroyed.

phases.title: Into India
phases.description: The monsoon breaks; the troops march through the Kabaw valley to Tamu and IV Corps takes command.

perspectives.name: William Slim
perspectives.objective: Hold the Irrawaddy front and the oilfields with the Chinese, then bring Burma Corps out to India intact.
perspectives.known: His corps was improvised and short of staff, the air had been lost, and the Japanese were moving round his flanks with road blocks.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Chinese would attack when and where they agreed, and whether the army could reach the Chindwin before the Japanese and the monsoon.
perspectives.constraints: No air cover, a single track to the Chindwin, too few river steamers, and wounded and refugees who had to come with the army.
perspectives.decision: He held the oilfields until the last moment, used the Chinese 38th Division to relieve the trapped 1st Burma Division, blocked the Myittha valley, and brought the corps out through Shwegyin at the cost of its guns and vehicles.
perspectives.forces: Burma Corps: the 1st Burma Division, the 17th Indian Division and the 7th Armoured Brigade, with the Chinese 38th Division under command in April.
perspectives.terrain: The dry Irrawaddy valley, then the Yeu–Shwegyin track and the Chindwin.
perspectives.logistics: Staging camps stocked along the track; petrol to the last; nearly all equipment destroyed at Shwegyin.
perspectives.outcome: Burma was lost, but the corps reached India without losing its cohesion.

perspectives.name: Shojiro Iida
perspectives.objective: Destroy the Allied armies in central Burma in a decisive battle for Mandalay and occupy the whole country.
perspectives.known: He had more divisions in Burma than the Allies believed, command of the air, and divisions able to move fast round the flanks of road-bound enemies.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Allies would stand to fight in the Irrawaddy loop or slip away.
perspectives.constraints: The British and Chinese fronts lay in separate valleys divided by the Pegu Yomas, and he had planned for the decisive battle to be over by the middle of May.
perspectives.decision: When the Allies escaped the trap at Mandalay, he ordered his four divisions on 26 April to strike wide and deep behind them to cut their lines of retreat.
perspectives.forces: The Fifteenth Army's four divisions.
perspectives.terrain: The Irrawaddy and Sittang valleys and the Shan States.
perspectives.logistics: Motor transport and river craft behind fast-moving infantry.
perspectives.outcome: Burma was occupied and China's land route closed, but the British and part of the Chinese armies escaped to India.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the retreat from Burma in May 1942 Wavell planned to return in the next dry season. His despatch records that the heavy monsoon, malaria and the Congress disturbances of August and September in India delayed preparations, and that operations in Madagascar took the troops, ships and landing craft needed for a seaborne expedition. By the middle of November he had abandoned hope of taking Akyab from the sea and decided to try an advance from Chittagong down the Arakan coast to the Mayu peninsula, from which the island could be attacked at short range.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Wavell writes that the operations had one objective only, Akyab island, and that he would not have committed troops to the unhealthy Arakan jungles had he had the naval and air forces and landing craft for a seaborne assault; sooner than keep his troops idle, he took the risk with troops who were not fully trained or equipped. He expected the Chinese in Yunnan and IV Corps in Assam to keep the Japanese in Upper Burma busy, but the Chinese made no move and IV Corps could do little, so the Japanese could reinforce Arakan.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Under the plan Wavell gave Irwin's Eastern Army on 19 November, the 14th Indian Division under Lloyd was to advance overland down the Mayu peninsula, from whose tip a short-range assault on Akyab could be made with small craft. When Slim's XV Corps took command on 14 April 1943, the aim had become defensive: Slim's first operation instruction made it his object to hold the Maungdaw–Tunnels area, with Buthidaung to be held unless that endangered the main object.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Kirby describes Arakan as densely forested parallel hill ranges separated by narrow valleys of ricefields cut by tidal chaungs. The coastal strip of the Mayu peninsula narrows to a few hundred yards in the south between Donbaik and Foul Point and is flanked by the steep Mayu Range, crossed in 1942 by a single metalled road from Maungdaw to Buthidaung through two tunnels. The tidal chaungs were obstacles to tanks and, at high tide, to infantry. In the monsoon wheeled traffic stopped.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The advance was made by the 14th Indian Division, reinforced brigade by brigade, with Irwin giving Lloyd his orders. Slim's XV Corps, responsible for the defence of Bengal, took command in Arakan only on 14 April 1943; Kirby records that when Irwin ordered XV Corps to send forward a few Valentine tanks for the attack on Donbaik in February, Slim pointed out that they were too few, a view that was not accepted. On the Japanese side Koga's 55th Division, Kirby notes, had fought throughout the 1942 campaign. Madan says most of the Indian brigades had had practically no anti-malarial training and that reinforcements arrived untrained.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The advance began in the autumn of 1942. The Japanese withdrew from the Maungdaw–Buthidaung line, which the British occupied in mid-December, and the 14th Division pushed down both sides of the Mayu Range. In January it reached the Japanese positions at Donbaik, near the tip of the peninsula, and at Rathedaung on the Mayu River, which the Japanese had fortified and held.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Repeated attacks on Donbaik and Rathedaung from January to mid-February failed against well-sited, concealed bunkers, including the February attack with tanks. At the end of February Irwin accepted Lloyd's view that further attacks were unjustified, but at Wavell's wish a last attack on Donbaik was made on 18 March and failed. The reinforced Japanese then crossed the Mayu River and the range and struck the exposed flank of the troops on the peninsula; on 29 March Irwin countermanded Lloyd's order to withdraw, relieved him, and took command until Lomax arrived. Lomax extricated one brigade by the beach road; another broke into small groups and made its way out through the jungle without its equipment. In April the Japanese drove north; XV Corps took command on 14 April, and in early May the Japanese broke through on the range, Buthidaung was abandoned and Maungdaw was then given up. The British ended in May back where they had started in October 1942.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Wavell chose to attempt Akyab overland rather than wait for the means of a seaborne attack, and then to renew the attack on Donbaik in March. Irwin held on in the peninsula after its flank was exposed and countermanded Lloyd's withdrawal. Slim, taking over with troops whose morale he judged generally poor and in some units very low, wrote in an appreciation of 24 April that lines of defence in such country could always be turned, and that what was needed were strong, well-stocked pivots from which striking forces could destroy the enemy; he proposed to withdraw to the open Cox's Bazar area and let the Japanese string themselves out, writing: “Let him. Pursuing this policy we give the Japanese all the dirty work.” Irwin insisted that Maungdaw be held; on 8 May they compromised on giving up Maungdaw but holding a line from Bawli Bazar to Taung Bazar.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Kirby identifies the failures at Donbaik and Rathedaung, which gave the Japanese time to bring up a well-trained division, as the turning point. Koga avoided frontal attacks and, using the central position and his control of the rivers, manoeuvred first the 14th and then the 26th Division out of their positions by deep outflanking attacks on their communications. In early May Lomax's plan to trap the advancing Japanese in a box on the Mayu Range failed; Slim reported to Irwin that the sides of the box had crumbled and the lid had opened without adequate reason, mainly because of the very low morale of units long in Arakan without relief.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Wavell's despatch concedes that strategically the army failed to reach Akyab and finished where it started, that the capture of Akyab overland was always a gamble, and that the serious loss was in prestige and morale; the greatest gain was experience of the enemy's methods and of the army's own defects in training and organization. On 20 May Wavell replaced Irwin, who had been in ill health for some time, with Giffard.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign left the army in Arakan with its morale low, malaria widespread and the Japanese confirmed in their belief that British and Indian troops could be levered out of any position by cutting their communications. Slim's XV Corps held the monsoon line in 1943, and Madan records his instructions in June and October for the next season's operations. Kirby judges that the well-conceived plans prepared by Slim and Lomax might have succeeded with determined troops, and that morale could have been restored only by withdrawing the units that had been in Arakan too long.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Kirby draws the lesson that frontal attacks on well dug-in and skilfully sited positions never succeeded in Burma without overwhelming artillery or close support by tanks and aircraft, and that troops too dependent on their communications were levered out by an enemy who went round them. An offensive begun with partly trained troops at the end of a weak line of communication, and continued for prestige after its object had gone, cost more than the ground was worth. A commander who arrives at the end of a failing campaign can conduct its withdrawal and draw its lessons, but cannot reverse it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Wavell wrote that on balance he would never regret ordering the campaign despite the lack of resources. Kirby, writing later with access to the records, judges that Wavell might have been well advised to cancel the attempt on Akyab once the initiative passed to the Japanese, that his order for a further attack on Donbaik in March was courting disaster, and that Irwin's instructions to Lomax showed how far his views were from the realities of the situation. Madan's Indian history emphasizes the troops' fatigue, malaria and lack of training. The casualty figure Wavell gives is not used here, and the Japanese side is told through Kirby's use of Japanese records.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Kirby's British official history gives the terrain, the narrative from both sides, Slim's appreciation and a critical review of the campaign. Madan's Indian official history gives the operations brigade by brigade and the troops' condition. Wavell's two despatches give the commander-in-chief's reasons for the campaign and his verdict on it.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: A year after the failure of the first Arakan offensive, XV Indian Corps under Christison, part of Slim's Fourteenth Army, advanced again on the Mayu peninsula. Maungdaw fell on 9 January 1944, and the corps was regrouping for a deliberate attack on the Japanese defences east of the Mayu Range. The 5th Indian Division held the coastal side of the range and the 7th Indian Division the Kalapanzin valley to the east, linked by a road over the Ngakyedauk Pass.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Monograph No. 132, compiled after the war by former officers of the Japanese 28th Army, describes the Ha-Go offensive as a diversion ordered by the Burma Area Army to be launched in Arakan two or three weeks before the U-Go offensive against Imphal. Kirby writes that its ultimate object was to draw in and hold Fourteenth Army's reserves in Arakan while the Fifteenth Army overran the Imphal plain. Slim, for his part, judged that the self-confidence of his troops would be restored only if the unbroken run of Japanese success with infiltration and envelopment was ended, and he could not risk even a minor defeat at the start of the 1944 campaign.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Hanaya, commanding the Japanese 55th Division, expected a British offensive in February or March and decided to forestall it. His Sakurai Column was to pass round the British left east of the Kalapanzin, seize Taung Bazar, block the Ngakyedauk Pass and destroy the 7th Indian Division from the rear; the 5th Indian Division was then to be destroyed in turn. Slim had already told his commanders that any unit whose communications were cut was to stand fast and attack its attackers' communications; he would supply it by air and bring up reserves to destroy the enemy in its rear.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought in an area about ten miles square between the Mayu Range and the tidal Kalapanzin River, crossed by jungle-clad ridges with small ricefields between them. Sinzweya, the 7th Division's administrative area, lay in an amphitheatre about a mile long surrounded by jungle-covered hills, with Ammunition Hill jutting into it. Morning mist and the noise of dew falling on dry undergrowth hid movement in the jungle, and knife-edge ridges made it hard for artillery to reach Japanese positions on reverse slopes.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: XV Corps had the 5th and 7th Indian Divisions forward, a regiment of medium tanks, and the 26th Indian Division and part of the 36th Division in reserve further back; the 81st West African Division was in the Kaladan valley. Hanaya divided the 55th Division into columns: one under Major-General Sakurai, built on the 112th Regiment under Colonel Tanahashi, to make the envelopment, and another under Colonel Doi to hold the defences west of the river. Above them, Lieutenant-General Shozo Sakurai's 28th Army sanctioned the plan. Spitfires newly arrived in the theatre gave the Allies the means to contest the air.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On the evening of 3 February XV Corps was completing its regrouping for an attack due between 6 and 8 February. The Sakurai Column moved through the British lines in the darkness and mist of the early hours of 4 February. Kirby says it achieved almost complete surprise, partly because XV Corps had paid too little heed to information from forward troops in late January; within a day it was deployed behind the 7th Division.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 6 February the 7th Division's headquarters was overrun, and Messervy and his staff fought their way out to Sinzweya, where the administrative troops, divisional troops and part of a brigade formed the Admin Box. The pass was blocked, and from 8 February Christison called for air supply for all formations east of the range; supply dropping began on 9 February, by night after enemy fighters appeared. On the night of 7–8 February the Japanese overran the main dressing station in the box and killed wounded men and medical staff before they were driven out. The other brigades dug in on their positions and held. From 16 February the 26th and 5th Divisions pressed on the Japanese rear and towards the pass. On 22 February, without food or ammunition, Tanahashi decided on his own authority to withdraw; the pass was reopened on 23–24 February, on the 24th Hanaya called off the offensive, and on 26 February the corps' communications were clear.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: On the evening of 4 February Slim, at Christison's request, put a brigade of the 26th Division at XV Corps' disposal and told Christison that his formations would be supplied by air if necessary; the next day he gave him the whole division. Giffard records that he placed the 36th Division at Slim's disposal, and that Slim ordered all forward formations to hold their ground and had rations, ammunition and medical stores packed for delivery by air. Kirby notes that a small Japanese raiding force on the Bawli–Maungdaw road drew off the first reserves to come forward, delaying the striking force for days. On the Japanese side, Tanahashi's withdrawal without his superior's sanction made the end of the offensive certain; the monograph says Major-General Sakurai was extremely angry but later accepted that lack of food had made it inevitable.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The boxes did not break. Kirby writes that the Sinzweya garrison, largely administrative troops, fought magnificently and, helped by poorly co-ordinated Japanese attacks, repelled every attempt to break in. Air supply let encircled troops stand instead of retreating; Saunders argues it was made possible by the Spitfires' success in the air, while Madan calls it an innovation for Burma. The Japanese column, whose communications were precarious, ran short of food and ammunition from about mid-February, according to Japanese records cited by Kirby.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Ha-Go offensive was abandoned and the remnants of the Sakurai Column withdrew. Giffard calls the defence the first successful reply to Japanese large-scale infiltration tactics in jungle country, and the basic reason for the victory the refusal of the troops to waver. XV Corps resumed its offensive in March, taking Buthidaung and Razabil, and the 5th Indian Division was then moved by air to the Imphal front.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Kirby judges that had the 7th Division been overwhelmed, Fourteenth Army's morale would have suffered seriously and it would have been impossible to move major formations from Arakan to the central front; instead the battle showed there was an answer to Japanese envelopment and gave the troops confidence in their leaders and in themselves. Saunders writes that the tactics that saved the Admin Box were repeated on a larger scale at Imphal. The diversion did not hold Fourteenth Army's reserves in Arakan.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Encircled troops can hold if they are told beforehand that they will be supplied and reinforced, if the means of supply exist and if the air can be kept clear; the method failed where those conditions did not hold. An envelopment that depends on the enemy retreating fails when he stands, if its own supply depends on his giving way. Surprise was won through a failure to heed forward reports, and the reserves were slow to arrive; the method worked despite those faults, not because there were none.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Kirby calls the battle the turning point of the war in South-East Asia and the first time the Japanese met well-trained British and Indian formations; Madan calls the defence a turning point in the campaign. The Japanese monograph blames a Japanese tactical blunder, the belief that the main British force was bottled up at Sinzweya, and says the three British brigades nearby took no action, which let the column attack and then escape. Madan credits the box technique to South-East Asia Command, Kirby and Giffard to Slim's orders, and Saunders writes mostly of Mountbatten and the air force. The killings at the dressing station are told differently by the survivors Kirby and Madan cite. Saunders names the Japanese commander “General Hanayoa”. Casualty figures in the sources are not used here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Kirby's British official history gives the ground, the plans of both sides from their records, the battle and a critical commentary. Madan's Indian official history gives the boxes, the escape of the divisional headquarters and a survivor's account of the dressing station. Giffard's despatch gives the army group commander's account and verdict. Monograph No. 132 gives the 28th Army's view, written by its former staff officers. Saunders's air history gives the fight for the air and the supply dropping.

perspectives.known: In 1943 the same envelopment had levered the British out of every position they held.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the British would retreat again when their communications were cut.
perspectives.constraints: Inferior numbers, and columns behind the British lines with precarious communications.
perspectives.decision: He sent the Sakurai Column round the British flank to block the pass and attack from the rear, and called off the offensive on 24 February.

perspectives.outcome: The column was exhausted and withdrew; the offensive failed to hold British reserves in Arakan.
