sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Orde Wingate's first long-range penetration expedition into Burma in 1943, Kirby writes, the Prime Minister and the Chiefs of Staff at the Quadrant conference at Quebec in August 1943, deeply impressed by his theories, decided to increase his long-range penetration brigades from two to six. Auchinleck, then Commander-in-Chief India, protested that this broke up divisions needed for the main campaign and that such forces could not win decisive results on their own; he was overruled, and had to break up a battle-experienced British division and take a brigade from the newly arrived African division to find the men.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: By early 1944 the plans for a concentric offensive into Burma had shrunk. Kirby writes that Special Force was given the task of helping Stilwell's Chinese–American advance on Myitkyina by cutting the communications of the Japanese 18th Division, while Fourteenth Army made limited advances. Slim expected a Japanese offensive across the Chindwin and planned to fight it on the Imphal plain. Romanus and Sunderland write that Wingate's own hopes went much further: to concentrate brigades around Indaw, force the Japanese out of northern Burma and open the way for IV Corps to advance to the Chindwin, aims they call far different from Slim's plan to lure the Japanese to Imphal.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Special Force was to fly into clearings named Broadway, Piccadilly and Chowringhee north-east of Indaw, establish defended strongholds with airstrips, and from them cut the railway and roads running north to the 18th Division. Wingate planned that each brigade would choose a stronghold inaccessible to armour and heavy artillery as a base for raiding columns. Slim agreed, but told him to learn from IV Corps' method of keeping mobile detachments outside defended areas. When Wingate asked for four extra battalions to garrison the strongholds, Slim agreed to have one battalion ready and three more trained, but kept the decision whether and when to fly them in to himself.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The landing grounds lay in jungle clearings between the Irrawaddy and the railway from Mandalay to Myitkyina, which carried supplies to the Japanese in the north. Strongholds were meant to be in country the enemy could not reach with tanks and guns; White City, the block on the railway near Mawlu, was not. Monsoon rains began in May and turned the operation into a struggle with disease and exposure as well as the enemy.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Special Force, given the cover name of 3rd Indian Division though it included few Indian troops, had five brigades in action, largely drawn from the British 70th Division, with a West African brigade and Kachin levies; No. 1 Air Commando of the U.S. Army Air Forces gave it fighters, bombers and transports. It was under Slim's command until it passed to Stilwell on 17 May. Against it the Japanese at first gathered scratch units under Mutaguchi's Fifteenth Army, then battalions drawn from several divisions, an independent mixed brigade and the arriving 53rd Division; the new 33rd Army was formed in April partly to deal with it.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On the afternoon of 5 March Slim, Wingate and the air commanders met at Lalaghat to see the 77th Brigade off. Half an hour before take-off, photographs from a reconnaissance flight sent without Wingate's knowledge showed Piccadilly blocked with tree trunks. Fearing betrayal, they considered calling the operation off; Calvert, commanding the brigade, was willing to go on, and the final decision lay with Slim. He judged that the blocking did not necessarily mean the Japanese knew the plan, that cancelling would throw his campaign plan out of gear, and that he had promised Stilwell to cut the 18th Division's communications. The whole brigade was sent to Broadway that night, just over an hour late.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Many gliders crashed on the rutted strip at Broadway, but American engineers had it ready for transports, and the fly-in of the 77th and 111th Brigades was complete by 11 March, with a third brigade marching in from Ledo. The 77th Brigade set up White City on the railway near Mawlu and held it against repeated attacks. On 24 March Wingate was killed when the American bomber carrying him crashed in the mountains west of Imphal; Slim appointed Lentaigne, the most experienced of his brigadiers, to succeed him. In April the force was moved north to support Stilwell, and on 17 May it passed to his command. Between 22 and 26 June the 77th Brigade and the Chinese 114th Regiment took Mogaung, and both claimed the credit. The exhausted brigades were then withdrawn.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Slim's decision of 5 March to go ahead despite the blocked landing ground kept the operation alive. Mutaguchi, told on 9 March of the landings, judged them a diversion heralding a counter-attack and held to his Imphal offensive, though the chief of staff of the 5th Air Division and some Fifteenth Army staff officers urged that it be reconsidered. Kirby judges that after the landings Wingate abandoned his own precepts, using his brigades to attack strongly defended places as if they were normal formations, with Indaw airfield an obsession. When Wingate gave the 14th Brigade orders that cut across Slim's plan, Kirby says he either misread Slim's wishes again or deliberately pursued his own; Slim ordered the brigade used as planned. Slim's choice of Lentaigne, and the transfer of the force to Stilwell, decided how the rest of it was spent.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The cutting of the railway was the operation's main effect. Romanus and Sunderland write that the Japanese had suspended supply to the 18th Division in January to build up stocks for Imphal, so that when the Chindits cut the line the division had to live on what it had, its supply position fundamentally compromised. The battalions sent against the Chindits were drawn from their parent units at key places. When the force came under Stilwell and was used as ordinary infantry through the monsoon, Kirby writes, malaria, exertion on short rations and exposure wore it down until it became completely ineffective.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Japanese communications to the north were cut for months, and Mogaung fell. Giffard wrote in June 1945 that the operations had less effect than he had hoped: they did not affect the launching of the Japanese offensive against Assam, had little effect on its communications, delayed only a few battalions of the 15th Division on their way to Imphal, and drew off only one battalion from Stilwell's front, so that the results did not prove commensurate with the manpower and material spent.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Kirby judges that the operation did little to help Fourteenth Army defeat the Japanese offensive, and even hampered it, because supplying five brigades by air aggravated the shortage of aircraft; a fresh Japanese division brought in partly to deal with the Chindits provided reinforcements for the Fifteenth Army. The Japanese monograph draws a different conclusion: that the airborne force upset the Fifteenth Army's timetable, kept its headquarters from moving forward until late April, cut the supply routes of two of its divisions and eventually led to the abandonment of northern Burma.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A force behind enemy lines can cut communications when air supply and air cover hold, but it cannot hold ground against an enemy who brings up guns and armour, and it wears out quickly if it is used as ordinary infantry. A subordinate with a direct line to the head of government, whose aims differ from his commander's, can be employed only by setting firm limits on what he is given; Slim kept the decision on reinforcements to himself. The cost fell on the men who marched through the monsoon on short rations and on the aircraft taken from the main battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The value of the operation is disputed in the sources themselves. Kirby, writing for the British official history, is severe on Wingate's methods and finds that Auchinleck's objections were proved sound; Giffard found the results not worth the cost. The Japanese monograph credits the airborne force with upsetting the Imphal offensive and losing the Japanese northern Burma, and Romanus and Sunderland call the diversion a great aid to Stilwell. Kirby records that after his meeting with Slim in January Wingate told Mountbatten that Slim had agreed to put four battalions at his disposal, which Slim's own messages of the time do not bear out. Giffard's tribute called Wingate a rare combination of the dreamer and the man of action. Troop figures in the sources are not used here.

sections.text: Kirby's British official history gives the planning, the Slim–Wingate exchanges, the fly-in, Wingate's death and a critical retrospect. Romanus and Sunderland give the American view of Wingate's aims, the effect on the Japanese 18th Division and the fall of Mogaung. Giffard's despatch gives the army group commander's verdict, and Monograph No. 134 the Fifteenth Army's reaction and its own assessment.

perspectives.name: Orde Wingate
perspectives.objective: Use long-range penetration brigades, supplied by air from strongholds, to dislocate the Japanese in northern Burma and open the way for a general advance.
perspectives.known: His 1943 expedition had shown that columns could move and be supplied behind the Japanese lines; he had the backing of the Prime Minister and an air commando of his own.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Japanese knew of the plan after a landing ground was found blocked, and how they would react.
perspectives.constraints: An army commander who kept the reinforcements under his own control, a role limited to helping Stilwell, and the coming monsoon.

perspectives.outcome: He was killed on 24 March; his force cut the railway but was worn out under Stilwell.

perspectives.name: Renya Mutaguchi
perspectives.objective: Carry through the Imphal offensive and keep the airborne force from disrupting it.
perspectives.known: An enemy airborne force had landed north and south-east of Katha on 5 March.
perspectives.uncertainty: How strong the force was; his own staff underrated it while the air division and the Burma Area Army took it more seriously.
perspectives.constraints: Troops already committed to Imphal, so that the force had to be met with scratch units and battalions taken from other divisions.
perspectives.decision: He judged the landings a diversion before a counter-attack, held to the Imphal offensive and sent improvised units against the airborne force.
perspectives.forces: Composite units and battalions from several divisions, later the 24th Independent Mixed Brigade and the 53rd Division.
perspectives.terrain: The railway corridor between Indaw and Myitkyina.
perspectives.logistics: Supply to the 18th Division cut, and his headquarters held back by the threat to its rear.
perspectives.outcome: The Imphal offensive went ahead, but the airborne force cut his communications and the Japanese lost northern Burma.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Imphal and Kohima the Fourteenth Army followed the Japanese across the Chindwin. Its plan for the 1944–1945 dry season, Operation CAPITAL, was to bring the Japanese armies to battle and destroy them on the Shwebo plain between the Chindwin and the Irrawaddy, north of Mandalay. Kimura, the new commander of the Burma Area Army, decided not to defend so far north, reasoning, MacGarrigle writes, that the Allies' supply problems would grow as they advanced south while his own eased; early in December Slim began to suspect it.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Allied priorities were set elsewhere: Slim's revised plan of 17 and 20 December assumed that combat cargo squadrons would be moved from Burma to China and that no formation could be moved by air. Its object remained the destruction of the Japanese forces in Burma; its immediate aim was to make them fight in central Burma, where his own communications were shorter, and, for administrative reasons, to take a port in south Burma between March and May, before the monsoon.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Under the new plan, which Slim called EXTENDED CAPITAL, XXXIII Corps was to close up to the Irrawaddy and encircle Mandalay, while IV Corps moved up the Myittha valley, crossed the Irrawaddy near Pakokku and seized Meiktila and Thazi. Kirby explains why: Meiktila and Thazi were the key points on the road and railway from Mandalay to Rangoon and the main Japanese administrative area in central Burma, so the Japanese would have to fight to clear them. Leese's despatch adds that Meiktila held their principal airfields and that all their communications radiated from it.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Below Mandalay lies what Leese calls the more open country of the Dry Belt, with Meiktila set among large lakes that narrowed the approaches. The Irrawaddy was wide: at the Nyaungu crossing more than a mile, with a wide sandy beach on the far side. IV Corps' route lay down the Gangaw and Myittha valleys, a long approach on which its divisions made their own roads. Mandalay's Fort Dufferin was a walled enclosure a mile square.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Slim commanded the Fourteenth Army under Leese's Allied Land Forces South-East Asia. XXXIII Corps under Stopford and IV Corps under Messervy each had tank brigades; the 17th Indian Division under Cowan made the dash to Meiktila. Kimura's Burma Area Army had the 15th Army under Katamura holding the Irrawaddy front, the 33rd Army under Honda to the north-east and the 28th Army in the south-west, with units of the Indian National Army on the river near Pagan.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: XXXIII Corps crossed the Irrawaddy north of Mandalay in January and west of it in February, drawing the Japanese counter-attacks. Meanwhile IV Corps moved south through the Gangaw valley. Leese describes the deception measures meant to persuade the Japanese that IV Corps was still on XXXIII Corps' left and that movement in the Gangaw valley was a small demonstration. On 14 February the 7th Indian Division began crossing near Nyaungu; at Pagan an Indian National Army company that had been left to hold the town surrendered to the Sikhs crossing to it.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: By 16 February the Nyaungu bridgehead was clear. On 21 February the 17th Division and a tank brigade broke out for Meiktila, supplied by air, and on 3 March cleared the town against a garrison that included hospital patients put into the defences. The Japanese then concentrated every unit they could to retake it, and through March Meiktila was besieged while its garrison struck out. In the north XXXIII Corps reached Mandalay early in March; on 20 March, after the remnants of the garrison had withdrawn in the night, Burmese civilians came out of Fort Dufferin under a white flag to say that no Japanese were left. On 28 March the Burma Area Army's chief of staff agreed to abandon the counter-offensive at Meiktila, and by the end of the month the battles were over.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Slim's decision of mid-December to scrap CAPITAL for EXTENDED CAPITAL was the decisive one: having concluded from air reconnaissance, captured documents and reports from villagers that the Japanese meant to withdraw, he moved his main blow south. Kirby gives the main credit for the crossing at Nyaungu to Messervy and his commanders, who took risks and let nothing delay them. On the Japanese side, Kimura agreed in February to Katamura's plan for a counter-offensive against the expected thrust near Mandalay, and a conference at Meiktila judged that any thrust from Nyaungu would be on the scale of a Chindit raid. Katamura gave up the defence of Mandalay in mid-March when Meiktila made it pointless.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Kirby attributes the swift success at Nyaungu to the thrust striking the junction of the 15th and 28th Armies and to deception that fixed Japanese attention on Mandalay and made them think the Myittha valley threat was a diversion west of the river. The fall of Meiktila on 3 March cut the communications of the Japanese armies to the north; MacGarrigle writes that the drive on to Thazi cut off the Japanese troops north of it from their supplies and their best line of retreat. Saunders adds that fighters kept Japanese reconnaissance aircraft away from the Gangaw valley to hide IV Corps' move. The failure of the Japanese counter-offensive, in which their divisions lost most of their guns, decided the battle.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Kirby writes that the 15th and 33rd Armies suffered a major defeat and that the Burma Area Army had virtually ceased to exist as a fighting force. Mandalay was occupied on 20 March. The road south to Rangoon lay open, and the Fourteenth Army turned to race the monsoon.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: With the Japanese armies in central Burma broken, the Fourteenth Army could advance down the railway and the Irrawaddy towards Rangoon before the monsoon closed the airfields and the roads. By the time Mandalay fell, MacGarrigle notes, the American Mars Task Force and the Chinese forces had finished fighting in Burma and began to return to China.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A plan built for one enemy course of action can be changed in time if the commander reads the signs early and his army can move faster than the enemy can read the change; the change here depended on air supply, engineers who built roads and ferries, and deception. Striking at a base the enemy must recover forces him to fight on ground he did not choose. The success also depended on Japanese misjudgements, and it was won at the cost of towns and villages fought over in central Burma.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources tell the plan differently. Kirby prints Slim's telegrams and appreciation and credits the change of plan to him; Leese's despatch, written as army group commander, presents the selection of Meiktila in his own voice. MacGarrigle's American brochure emphasizes that the armoured column was supplied entirely by air and that aerial resupply played a decisive role, and Saunders's air history argues that without air supremacy the plan could not but have failed; Saunders also praises the speed and skill with which Kimura concentrated against the crossings at Myinmu before IV Corps confounded him. The Japanese side is told through Kirby's use of Japanese records; the monographs on the 1945 operations were not readable here, and the Fifteenth Army's monograph ends in January 1945. Loss and prisoner figures in the sources are not used.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Kirby's British official history gives Slim's plan, the crossings, Meiktila, Mandalay and the Japanese conferences and orders from their records. Leese's despatch gives the army group view of the plan and the battle. MacGarrigle's brochure gives the American and Chinese context and the air supply. Monograph No. 134 gives the Fifteenth Army's withdrawal to the Irrawaddy up to January 1945. Saunders's air history gives the air supply, the air cover over IV Corps' approach and a view of Kimura's generalship.

perspectives.name: William Slim
perspectives.objective: Destroy the Japanese armies in central Burma and reach a south Burma port before the monsoon.
perspectives.known: Reconnaissance, captured documents and villagers' reports showed the Japanese withdrawing behind the Irrawaddy and not preparing to fight on the Shwebo plain.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Japanese would withdraw from Burma, cover the southern ports or counter-attack when he was extended.
perspectives.constraints: Transport aircraft taken for China, no airborne force, and the monsoon in May.
perspectives.decision: He sent IV Corps in secret down the Myittha valley to cross near Pakokku and seize Meiktila, while XXXIII Corps drew the Japanese to Mandalay.
perspectives.forces: The Fourteenth Army: XXXIII and IV Corps with two tank brigades.
perspectives.terrain: The Gangaw and Myittha valleys, the Irrawaddy and the open Dry Belt.
perspectives.logistics: Air supply for the striking force, roads built by the army, and ferries across the Irrawaddy.
perspectives.outcome: Meiktila and Mandalay fell, and the Japanese armies in central Burma were broken.

perspectives.name: H. Kimura
perspectives.objective: Hold southern Burma and defeat the British attempt to cross the Irrawaddy.
perspectives.known: The Allies' supply problems would grow as they advanced south; the British were crossing near Mandalay, and his intelligence expected their main thrust there.
perspectives.uncertainty: What force was moving through the Myittha valley, which the majority at the Meiktila conference judged no larger than a Chindit raid.
perspectives.constraints: Armies depleted by the defeat at Imphal and spread along a long river line.
perspectives.decision: He withdrew behind the Irrawaddy, approved a counter-offensive near Mandalay, and then threw every unit he could gather against Meiktila.
perspectives.forces: The 15th, 33rd and 28th Armies, with Indian National Army units.
perspectives.terrain: The Irrawaddy line and the communications centred on Meiktila.
perspectives.logistics: His main administrative base and airfields at Meiktila.
perspectives.outcome: Meiktila was lost and not retaken; his armies in central Burma were defeated.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the end of March 1945 the Japanese armies in central Burma had been defeated at Meiktila and Mandalay. Rangoon, the capital and the port through which the Fourteenth Army hoped to be supplied in the monsoon, lay some three hundred miles to the south. Kirby writes that from its commander downwards the army sensed that victory lay close ahead and that Rangoon could be reached in the short time left before the rains.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The advance depended on air supply, and Saunders writes that the capture of Rangoon had to be achieved by the end of May, when the American transport aircraft were to be withdrawn. Burmese politics were changing behind the Japanese lines: the Anti-Fascist Organization and the Burma National Army, commanded by Aung San, who had collaborated with the Japanese, began to rise against the Japanese about 27 March. Kirby records that Slim and Leese wanted the rising supported as an operational priority and that Mountbatten agreed, while the War Cabinet insisted that its leaders, as former collaborators, be told they would have to work their passage home and must not be treated as liberators of their country.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: IV Corps was to drive south down the railway from Meiktila through Pyawbwe and Toungoo to Pegu and Rangoon, and XXXIII Corps down the Irrawaddy valley. On 19 March Slim warned that the delays at Meiktila might stop him reaching Rangoon overland before the monsoon and recommended an amphibious attack on the city early in May as an insurance; Kirby notes that the initiative for a modified Operation DRACULA came from the Fourteenth Army. Mountbatten decided on 2 April to carry it out, with XV Corps' 26th Indian Division landing from the sea and a parachute battalion dropping at Elephant Point. Slim also ordered a fifteen-day stockpile built as far forward as Myingyan in case Rangoon could not be taken before the monsoon.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: From Meiktila the road and railway ran south through the Sittang valley to Toungoo, Pegu and Rangoon, with the Pegu Yomas, a forested range, between them and the Irrawaddy valley. The airfields at Toungoo were vital to the air support of the advance and of DRACULA. In April came the first pre-monsoon showers; when the monsoon proper broke it would flood rivers and airfields and stop movement off the all-weather roads.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Slim's Fourteenth Army advanced with IV Corps under Messervy, led by the 17th and 5th Indian Divisions with a tank brigade, and XXXIII Corps under Stopford; Christison's XV Corps in Arakan mounted DRACULA under Leese's land forces command. On the Japanese side Kimura's Burma Area Army had the remnants of the 15th and 33rd Armies in the east and the 28th Army in the Irrawaddy valley, with a Rangoon Defence Force formed from rear-area units, convalescents and trainees.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Kimura planned to hold a line from Loikaw through Toungoo to Prome, with the 33rd Army covering the 15th Army's withdrawal from the Mandalay battlefield. The 17th Division attacked the Japanese positions at Pyawbwe, which was surrounded by the evening of 9 April and taken in the only large action of the advance. Kirby writes that the speed of the Allied advance made Kimura's plans ineffective: Pyinmana was overrun before the 15th Army could reach it.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: After Pyawbwe the advance went south down the main road; Toungoo airfield was taken on 22 April, three days ahead of schedule, and aircraft were soon flying from it. The headquarters of the Burma Area Army left Rangoon for Moulmein on 23 April. The 17th Division reached Pegu at the end of April, found it held, and cleared it on 1 May. On the night of 2 May continuous torrential rain began, flooding the approaches to the new bridge over the Pegu River and the airfields at Toungoo. On 1 May a Gurkha parachute battalion took Elephant Point; on 2 May the seaborne landings went in unopposed, and the 26th Division entered Rangoon on 3 May. On 6 May it met the leading troops of the Fourteenth Army north of the city.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Slim's recommendation of 19 March, taken up by Leese and Mountbatten, gave the campaign its insurance. Slim decided early in April that he ought to meet Aung San so that the Burma National Army's activities could be co-ordinated with his own and kept under his orders. On the Japanese side Kimura ordered the 28th Army to defend Rangoon to the last, an order that could not be carried out; the 28th Army's commander, learning that Area Army headquarters had gone, moved his army into the Pegu Yomas, and the Japanese did not defend Rangoon.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The capture of the Toungoo airfields ahead of time kept air support and supply moving south; the Japanese defence at Pegu and the rain of 2 May stopped the Fourteenth Army short of the city. The Japanese decision to abandon Rangoon meant that DRACULA met almost no resistance. The air history records that a Mosquito pilot, Wing Commander A. E. Saunders, landed at Mingaladon on 2 May, found the airfield deserted and reached the gaol, where Allied prisoners of war had been left by their guards.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Rangoon was reoccupied before the monsoon. Saunders quotes Mountbatten's despatch: though the Fourteenth Army had technically lost the race, it was their drive that had really won the battle. MacGarrigle writes that by the end of May the Japanese forces in Burma were split into three groups, with the 28th Army trapped between the Irrawaddy and the Sittang.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The port could now supply the army through the monsoon. The Japanese left in the Pegu Yomas tried to break out across the Sittang in July and were destroyed, while Burmese guerrillas organized by Force 136 attacked the escaping troops. Aung San's forces had fought on the Allied side in the last weeks, and the questions the War Cabinet had raised about their place in a post-war Burma remained open.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A commander racing a deadline can ask for an insurance he hopes not to need; here the seaborne landing that Slim proposed took the city when the overland advance was stopped by rain a few days short. Speed broke the enemy's plans for successive defensive lines faster than he could man them. The rising of the Burmese resistance showed that an army returning to a colony could not settle on its own who would rule it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources differ on who won the race and on details of its end. Saunders, writing the air force's history, gives Mountbatten's verdict that the Fourteenth Army's drive won the battle and stresses air supply; Leese's despatch tells the operation from the army group's view. Saunders dates the departure of the gaol guards to 25 April, while Kirby gives 29 April and prints the note they left. Kirby's narrative of the Burmese rising follows British official papers, which treated Aung San as a former collaborator; neither the resistance's own records nor Burmese accounts were read for this study. Figures in the sources for losses and prisoners are not used.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Kirby's British official history gives the planning, the Burmese rising, the advance, the Japanese orders and the landings. Leese's despatch gives the army group commander's account. Saunders's air history gives the race with the monsoon, the air supply and the scene at Rangoon. MacGarrigle's brochure gives the position of the Japanese armies after the city fell.

perspectives.name: William Slim
perspectives.objective: Reach Rangoon before the monsoon and the withdrawal of the American transport aircraft.
perspectives.known: The Japanese in central Burma were beaten but would try to hold successive lines; his supply depended on aircraft that were due to leave.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the overland advance could reach Rangoon before the rains.
perspectives.constraints: Air supply, the delays caused at Meiktila, and a monsoon that would close the roads and airfields.
perspectives.decision: He drove IV Corps south down the railway as fast as it could go, built a stockpile in case it failed, and asked for a seaborne attack on Rangoon as insurance.
perspectives.forces: The Fourteenth Army: IV and XXXIII Corps.
perspectives.terrain: The Sittang valley road and railway, and the Irrawaddy valley.
perspectives.logistics: Air supply to airheads opened behind the advance, and the Toungoo airfields.
perspectives.outcome: His army was stopped by rain at Pegu, but the landing it had asked for took Rangoon.

perspectives.name: H. Kimura
perspectives.objective: Hold southern Burma on a line through Toungoo and defend Rangoon.
perspectives.known: His armies had been badly beaten at Meiktila and were retreating in disorder.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where the British would strike from the sea, and how fast their armour could move.
perspectives.constraints: Shattered divisions, scattered formations out of their commanders' control, and an air force reduced to almost nothing.
perspectives.decision: He planned successive holding lines, left Rangoon for Moulmein with his headquarters and ordered the 28th Army to hold the city, which it could not do.
perspectives.forces: The 15th, 33rd and 28th Armies and the Rangoon Defence Force.
perspectives.terrain: The Sittang valley and the Pegu Yomas.
perspectives.logistics: Supply dumps in Rangoon that the Allied air forces were bombing.
perspectives.outcome: Rangoon was abandoned and his armies split, the 28th Army trapped in the Pegu Yomas.
